title: Generally (Verdins)
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.1 – Generally (Verdins)
text: A court must take into account an offender’s impaired mental or intellectual functioning – whether it be the result of illness, injury, disability, or disorder, whether permanent or temporary, mild or severe, newly acquired or longstanding and whether the impairment existed at the time of the offending or at the time of sentencing. The Verdins principles do not depend on diagnostic labels: ‘What matters is what the evidence shows about the nature, extent and effect of the mental impairment experienced by the offender at the relevant time’. Specifically, how did it affect them at the time of the offending or how is it likely to impact their experience of imprisonment. In R v Verdins (‘Verdins’), the Court of Appeal identified six ways that mental impairment may be relevant to sentencing: 1. It may reduce an offender’s moral culpability and so affect what is considered to be a just punishment and lessen the need for denunciation; 2. It may have a bearing on the kind of sentence that is imposed and the conditions under which it should be served; 3. General deterrence may be moderated or eliminated as a consideration depending on the nature and severity of the offender’s symptoms, and the effect of their impairment at the time of offending, sentence, or both; 4. Specific deterrence may be similarly moderated or eliminated in the same circumstances; 5. The existence of an impairment at the time of sentencing, or its reasonably foreseeable reoccurrence, may mean that a specific sentence may weigh more heavily on the offender than it would on a person in normal health; 6. If there is a serious risk that imprisonment will have a significantly adverse impact on the offender’s mental health, this will be a mitigating factor. These Verdins ‘principles’ or ‘considerations’ may moderate both the minimum term and the head sentence, but they are exceptional and should not be invoked in routine cases. Lastly, a court is not required to run through and recite all of the Verdins principles as though exhausting a checklist.

title: Moral culpability
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability
text_marked:
The first Verdins principle says that if a mentally impaired offender is less morally culpable for their actions then it may not be appropriate to punish them as harshly as someone who is fully responsible.[^1140]
An offender’s moral culpability may be reduced if, at the time of the offence, their impairment:
• reduced their ability to exercise appropriate judgment, make calm and rational choices, think clearly, or appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct; or
• made them disinhibited; or
• obscured the intent to commit the offence; or
• contributed causally to the commission of the offence.[^1141]
This is not an exhaustive list - it is descriptive rather than prescriptive.[^1142]
The effect of an impairment on moral culpability is a matter of degree. A court should consider the gravity of the offending and, with the assistance of any expert evidence, the offender’s conduct before, during, and after the offending in order to determine the extent of the impairment’s contribution to the offending.[^1143] The relevant question is whether the evidence establishes that the impairment contributed in a way that made the offender ‘less blameworthy as a result’.[^1144] This is a discretionary assessment with no fixed guidelines,[^1145] although the High Court has said that there will usually be such a link if the offender is intellectually disabled.[^1146]
As noted, one way that moral culpability may be reduced is where there is a causal connection between the offender’s impairment and the offending conduct.[^1147] While a causal connection is not required by Verdins to reduce the offender’s culpability (or to moderate or eliminate general and specific deterrence),[^1148] some connection is still required. If the impairment existed at the time of the offending there must be a ‘realistic connection’ between the two, or the impairment must have ‘caused or contributed to’ or be ‘causally linked’ to the offending.[^1149]

path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability
text_marked:
If the offence is serious, an offender’s culpability may only be reduced to a minor extent, even if their impairment is significant.[^1150] Similarly, culpability may only be reduced to a limited extent where the offender was fully aware of the nature and gravity of what they were doing, and that it was wrong.[^1151] Planning and management of the offending and avoiding detection are indicative of such knowledge.[^1152]
A common feature of both Verdins and Bugmy[^1153] principles is that both permit a court to view the offender’s moral culpability as being reduced where their psychological functioning or personality structure has been impaired.[^1154] But it will require expert evidence to show how the two are connected,[^1155] and if there is convergence between the two care should be taken to avoid ‘inappropriate double counting’.[^1156] ‘[T]he principles identified in Bugmy must be considered in their own right quite apart from the impact of any mental impairment pursuant to Verdins principles’.[^1157]

text_marked:
An offender’s impairment may be relevant to the type of sanction imposed.[^1158] It may make some sanctions – such as imprisonment, where the offender’s mental impairment is significantly impacted, or they are unable to obtain treatment – inappropriate.[^1159]
There are specific statutory sanctions that are appropriate for offenders who are mentally impaired,[^1160] as well as alternatives to custodial terms that can be imposed for those offenders.[^1161]
However, while an offender’s impairment may be relevant to the kind of sentence imposed, the second Verdins principle does not say that a term of imprisonment cannot be imposed. It requires a court to consider the possibility by reference to the facts and circumstances of the case.[^1162]

title: General deterrence
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence
text_marked:
General deterrence may be moderated or eliminated if an offender suffers from an impairment at the time of offending, sentencing, or both.[^1163] But Verdins does not automatically require that general deterrence be modified where a person’s mental functioning is impaired.[^1164] The question is whether it should be moderated and that will depend on both the severity and nature of the condition and its effect on the offender’s mental capacity at the time of offending, sentencing, or both.[^1165] Generally, this means that some connection, which may be causal, between mental condition and the offending is required.[^1166]
Further, there must be an evidentiary basis to moderate general deterrence. It is not sufficient to find that an offender suffers from a mental impairment. There must be ‘proper and informed’ consideration of how the impairment materially diminished the offender’s capacity to reason appropriately about the wrongfulness of their conduct at the time of the offending, or how the offender’s condition might make full application of the principles of general deterrence repugnant to the humanitarian considerations that guide proper sentencing.[^1167]
Another consideration is whether the offender is an ‘appropriate vehicle’ for general deterrence. This may be determined by looking at whether the offender’s impairment would evoke the community’s sympathy and make people wonder why the offender is being punished.[^1168] A causal relationship between the impairment and the offending is usually sufficient to find that an offender is not an appropriate vehicle for general deterrence.[^1169] Although, this may not apply if the offender acted knowing that their conduct was wrong.[^1170]
The extent to which an impairment will moderate or eliminate general deterrence depends on three factors:
• the nature and severity of the symptoms exhibited by the offender;
• the effect of the condition on the mental capacity of the offender; and
• the nature and gravity of the offence.[^1171]

title: Specific deterrence
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.5 – Specific deterrence
text_marked:
One of the purposes of punishment is to specifically deter the offender from re-offending. This assumes the offender is capable of learning from the experience of punishment and can therefore be deterred from repeating the same or similar conduct. However, if the offender suffers from a mental impairment, ‘specific deterrence may be more difficult to achieve and is often not worth pursuing’.[^1175]
Whether and to what degree specific deterrence applies to an impaired offender depends on the circumstances.[^1176] Where the impairment makes them unable to accept their role in and responsibility for the offending, specific deterrence has little relevance.[^1177] But if an offender is able to appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct, specific deterrence is relevant.[^1178]
Specific deterrence should also not be moderated where the offender’s mental impairment arose as a reaction to the discovery of their crimes or the prospect of incarceration.[^1179]
Nor should it be moderated or eliminated if the court finds that imprisonment will actually have a specifically deterrent effect notwithstanding the offender’s impairment.[^1180]

title: Consequences of imprisonment
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.6 – Consequences of imprisonment
text_marked:
The consequences of imprisonment are relevant in sentencing a mentally impaired offender in two ways.
Firstly, imprisonment may weigh more heavily on an impaired offender than it would a person in normal health.[^1181] But in order to mitigate sentence on this basis it must be shown the impaired offender will suffer a significant additional burden. In determining this, a court should consider the nature of the custody. The burden of incarceration may be increased if the offender’s term will be served in isolation, protective custody, or under other circumscribed conditions,[^1182] or if the offender’s custodial placements are limited by the unavailability of appropriate treatment regimes.[^1183]
Secondly, a sentence should be mitigated if there is a ‘serious risk’ imprisonment will have a ‘significantly adverse effect’ on an offender’s mental health.[^1184] The deterioration that is likely to be caused by imprisonment must be greater than the mental deterioration that imprisonment generally causes any person to suffer.[^1185] In assessing the risk, a court should consider the history of the offender’s illness, the likely conditions of imprisonment, any difficulties in management presented by the offender, and the likelihood of the offender receiving treatment (and its effectiveness) while imprisoned.[^1186]
In either case, it does not matter that an offender’s mental impairment arose because their crimes were discovered or due to the prospect of incarceration. If their condition is likely to be aggravated by the experience of imprisonment, a court may reduce the offender’s sentence.[^1187] However, the weight to be given to these considerations always varies and does not displace consideration of the other sentencing purposes in the instinctive synthesis.[^1188]

text_marked:
The existence of the impairment alone or stress at the prospect of a prison term is not sufficient to mitigate the sentence.[^1189] The defence must establish the likely effect the offender’s impairment will have on the offender’s experience of imprisonment.[^1190] Where there is no evidence that prison would be more burdensome for the offender, or may worsen their condition, there is no need to moderate sentence.[^1191] It is open for the court to infer, in the absence of direct evidence, that a prisoner who suffers from a severe mental health condition would find prison more burdensome than another prisoner in normal health. However, whether that inference should be drawn depends on the totality of the evidence.[^1192]
Fresh evidence that an offender’s condition has deteriorated to a much greater degree than anticipated by the sentencing court may be admissible on appeal.[^1193]

The existence of the impairment alone or stress at the prospect of a prison term is not sufficient to mitigate the sentence. The defence must establish the likely effect the offender’s impairment will have on the offender’s experience of imprisonment. Where there is no evidence that prison would be more burdensome for the offender, or may worsen their condition, there is no need to moderate sentence. It is open for the court to infer, in the absence of direct evidence, that a prisoner who suffers from a severe mental health condition would find prison more burdensome than another prisoner in normal health. However, whether that inference should be drawn depends on the totality of the evidence. Fresh evidence that an offender’s condition has deteriorated to a much greater degree than anticipated by the sentencing court may be admissible on appeal.

title: Community protection
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.7 – Community protection
text_marked:
An offender’s mental impairment may reduce their culpability for an offence, but it may also make them a danger to society thereby increasing the importance of community protection as a sentencing consideration.[^1194]
Community protection is also important where an impaired offender has a significant criminal record,[^1195] or they understood that in stopping their medication there was a risk they would reoffend having done so previously,[^1196] or that substance abuse would lead to violent behaviour and yet continued to indulge.[^1197]
Where the offender is sentenced as a ‘serious offender’, the court must regard protection of the community as the principal sentencing purpose, despite the existence of a mental impairment.[^1198] But, as always, although community protection may be a key sentencing consideration, a court should not focus on one consideration to the exclusion of other relevant factors.[^1199]

title: Rehabilitation
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.8 – Rehabilitation
text_marked:
Mental impairment is relevant to the extent that it bears upon an offender’s prospects for rehabilitation.[^1200] It may also make rehabilitation the primary consideration where the other purposes (such as punishment, denunciation and deterrence) do not require significant emphasis because of the offender’s impairment.[^1201]
In such cases, a court may emphasise rehabilitation by setting a shorter than usual non-parole period so that treatment can be carried out at an earlier stage than usual. The relevant authorities may then also monitor the offender’s condition for a longer period of time once they are returned to the community. This course might be appropriate where the offender’s impairment cannot be properly treated or managed in a prison environment.[^1202]

title: Substance abuse
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.9 – Substance abuse
text_marked:
The mitigatory effect of mental impairment may be reduced where the condition is self-induced, often by drug or alcohol use. The key issue is what the offender knew about the possible consequences of taking the relevant substance,[^1203] what is required is foreknowledge that use of a substance ‘was likely to produce a delusional state’.[^1204] An offender’s culpability is unlikely to be reduced where they have a history of using substances known to lead to hallucinations and violence. Indeed, use of substances in that situation may be an aggravating factor.[^1205]
However, where the offender’s mental impairment and substance abuse are independent, the Verdins principles will continue to have full force,[^1206] meaning the considerations of denunciation and deterrence (general and specific) will have little role to play.[^1207]
Similarly, where the substance abuse is caused by the offender’s impairment, their moral culpability may be reduced, and the need for general and specific deterrence may be moderated.[^1208] But it is not enough to establish the impairment led to substance abuse. The defence must still prove that the impairment was connected to the offending.[^1209] In determining whether drug use was caused by an impairment, the court may take into account the quantity of drugs used.[^1210]
An offender cannot rely on a relapse of a pre-existing mental impairment as mitigating if it is caused by their failing to take prescribed medication or ingesting illegal drugs, but their moral culpability may still be reduced if another factor beyond their control - such as significant stress from the breakdown of a relationship or personal loss - also played some part in their relapse into a mentally impaired state.[^1211]

title: Personality disorders
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.10 – Personality disorders
text_marked:
The Verdins principles apply to personality disorders as they do to any other condition, there is no blanket exclusion of them from that framework.[^1212] But neither does the existence of such a disorder necessarily demonstrate impaired mental functioning.[^1213] The question of whether an offender’s personality disorder engages any of the Verdins principles does not depend on its particular diagnostic label, but on what the expert evidence before the court shows about how the condition affected the offender’s mental functioning at the time of the offending or how it will do so in the future.[^1214]
An offender with a diagnosed personality disorder stands in precisely the same position as any other offender who wishes to rely on impaired mental functioning in order to mitigate their sentence in one or more of the ways identified by Verdins, and any statement to the contrary in DPP (Vic) v O’Neill[^1215] should not be followed.[^1216]

title: Consideration and evidence
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence
text_marked:
Generally, a court only needs to consider the Verdins principles in cases where the issue is clearly raised by counsel,[^1217] and there is a sufficient evidentiary basis to do so.[^1218]
Defence counsel must submit evidence supporting a Verdins point advanced in mitigation, particularly when the court indicates that it is unpersuaded by their submissions. A court does not have an obligation to inquire into the evidence[^1219] or to make a factual inference about a mental impairment (unless there was a link between the impairment and the crime and a factual inference was the only conclusion reasonably open).[^1220] Similarly, there is no obligation for a court to consider the Verdins principles where defence counsel mentions the principles, but later retreats from reliance on them.[^1221]
The Verdins principles are six different, non-exhaustive, aspects of sentencing, so the nature and degree of a relevant impairment may be different depending on which aspect of the process is under consideration.[^1222] It is mechanistic, simplistic, and wrong to say that because an offender suffers from a mental impairment the Verdins principles apply. There has to be a careful and rigorous consideration of whether the evidence establishes that the offender’s mental capacity has been impaired and which of the circumstances identified in Verdins are applicable.[^1223]
There needs to be cogent evidence, normally in the form of expert evidence, establishing on the balance of the probabilities that the Verdins principles are enlivened.[^1224] The evidence must establish that the impairment existed at the time of offending, sentence, or both, as well as its nature, extent, and effect on the offender or its likely effect on them in the future.[^1225] Expert evidence also needs to be assessed against what is known about the circumstances of the offending.[^1226]
It is generally not sufficient for an expert to simply give evidence about the offender’s mental impairment. As noted, the Verdins principles do not depend on diagnostic labels, but on the impact of an impairment on the offender and the offender’s behaviour.[^1227]
Moreover, an impairment may have subtle abnormalities that affect perception and conduct and expert evidence on those subtleties will assist.[^1228]

title: Consideration and evidence
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence
text_marked:
While expert evidence is required, it is not determinative, and it is ultimately for the court, not a psychiatrist or psychologist, to decide if and how the Verdins principles apply in a given case.[^1229] It is wholly outside of a psychiatrist’s or psychologist’s expertise to express a view on whether one or more of the principles apply, and practitioners relying on expert reports should ensure they don’t contain impermissible opinions of that kind.[^1230] Expert evidence presented to support a Verdins argument should be a ‘legitimate expression of psychological opinion’ and should not include ‘unsubstantiated conclusions on matters [falling] clearly outside any psychologist’s expertise’.[^1231]
A court should be cautious before concluding that an offender suffered from a mental impairment at the relevant time, and that the impairment had one of the necessary effects.[^1232] Imprecision in expert opinions should signal to the court that it will be difficult to make a firm conclusion on their findings.[^1233]
A court’s assessment of the evidence must be rigorous and careful, and the prosecution plays an important part in identifying and challenging any inadequacy in the expert’s opinion or the circumstances on which it is formed.[^1234]
If a court is not inclined to accept the uncontested evidence of an expert,[^1235] or to only give it limited weight because the author of an expert report is not called to give evidence, it must give counsel notice of this and an opportunity to be heard.[^1236]

text_marked: As the Court of Appeal has noted, because many expert reports are self-serving and almost always based on self-reported information, a court has an obligation to carefully consider this evidence and must exercise great caution in determining if Verdins has been enlivened.[^1237] Thus, a court may reject an uncorroborated expert report based on self-reported information,[^1238] particularly if the report writer believes the offender was lying.[^1239] If the court accepts the evidence and concludes that one or more of the Verdins principles apply, its reasons should clearly explain the ways the impairment has been taken into account. It is not sufficient to merely refer to the competing submissions, or state that the offender’s impaired mental functioning affected the sentence without explaining how or to what extent.[^1240] Similarly, if a court concludes the evidence is inadequate to support an expert opinion and rejects an application of Verdins it must state its reasons for reaching that conclusion.[^1241]

title: Addictions
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions
text_marked:
Addictions, such as gambling addiction, drug addiction or alcoholism, can be relevant in several ways.
Firstly, addiction may bear on an offender’s moral culpability.[^1242] For example, it is relevant if the offender trafficked drugs in order to feed their own addiction rather than purely from greed and for profit.[^1243] But the weight to be attributed to this fact depends on the circumstances of each case and is greatly diminished, often to the point of non-existence, when considering trafficking operations above street level.[^1244] Similarly, an offender’s advantaged background, the way they were involved in a trafficking scheme, how they attempted to obtain a drug, and what they intended to do with it are all relevant to determining their culpability and may lessen any mitigating impact.[^1245]
Moreover, unless there is evidence to the contrary, it should be inferred that a person importing drugs is doing so for profit. The fact that an offender needs money to pay off a debt does not affect culpability, and their prior good character is given less weight in drug importation offences. Secondly, addiction is also relevant to rehabilitation, deterrence and community protection.[^1246] However, someone who has had repeated opportunities for reform should not reasonably expect to rely on addiction in mitigation.[^1247]
Lastly, an offender’s addiction may be relevant to the choice of sanction, either because it may qualify them for a sanction specifically tailored to their addiction or by emphasising the value of a general rehabilitative sanction.[^1248]

title: Intoxication
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.4 – Intoxication
text_marked:
Intoxication – whether through alcohol or narcotic consumption – will rarely mitigate offending,[^1249] and may even be an aggravating factor.[^1250] For intoxication to reduce moral culpability, the circumstances will have to be ‘quite exceptional’.[^1251] The key question is the degree of foreknowledge. If the offender knew of the likely consequences of drug ingestion their culpability is increased, and intoxication may be an aggravating factor.[^1252] Where a long history of alcohol consumption has not revealed the slightest indication that an offender poses a risk of violence, this may mean the circumstances are sufficiently exceptional to be mitigating.[^1253]
And as with addiction, intoxication may be relevant to sentencing purposes such as remorse and rehabilitation.[^1254]

title: Character
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character
text_marked:
‘Character’, ‘past history’, and ‘antecedents’ have been used synonymously and refer (at a minimum) to an offender’s previous criminal history. Under both the Victorian and Commonwealth regimes consideration of an offender’s character is required when determining the sentence to be imposed,[^1255] when deciding whether to exercise the discretion to record a State conviction,[^1256] and when fixing a non-parole period or making a recognizance release order.[^1257]
In determining an offender’s character, a court may consider:
• the number, seriousness, date, relevance and nature of any previous findings of guilt or convictions;[^1258]
• their general reputation;[^1259] and
• any significant contributions they’ve made to the community.[^1260]

title: Good character
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character
text_marked:
Good character is an established mitigating factor, but what makes a person of good character varies according to the individual and it impossible to state a universal rule.[^1261]
In determining whether an offender is of good character, a court must not consider the offending for which it is sentencing the offender. The issue at sentencing is whether, apart from the current offending, the person is otherwise of good character. If the evidence establishes that the offender is ‘otherwise of good character’ then, subject to a statutory exception, this must be taken into account in sentencing. However, the weight given to good character will vary according to the circumstances of the case and the offender,[^1262] and in determining the weight to be given to previous good character there is no prohibition on a court considering the nature and circumstances of the offending.[^1263]
A lack of similar prior convictions is 'a significant matter in mitigation'.[^1264] An offender’s prior good character will always entitle them to some leniency, although it may be minimal.[^1265] Good character must be balanced against the circumstances of the offence and the sentencing purposes.[^1266] The weight to be given to good character may depend on the seriousness of the offence and whether it was an isolated act or part of a course of conduct.[^1267] In the case of an offender charged with multiple offences the sentencer may attach less weight to previous good character.[^1268]
Good character is significant in cases of first offenders, particularly mature first offenders[^1269] or those acting under extraordinary external pressures.[^1270] But, again, this is qualified by the gravity of the offending and the other sentencing purposes.[^1271]
Good character is also relevant to an offender’s prospects of rehabilitation.[^1272]

text_marked: Good character will be of reduced significance for offences that are commonly committed by offenders of otherwise good character, or who exploit their respectability to further their offending.[^1273] Further, in sentencing for a child sexual offence, a court cannot consider an offender’s previous good character if the court is satisfied that their good character helped them commit the offence.[^1274] Factors such as breach of trust will similarly go to the weight to be given to the offender’s ‘otherwise good character’.[^1275] But undue weight cannot be given to an offender’s breach of trust. It cannot be used both as an aggravating factor and to diminish an offender’s good character.[^1276]

title: Bad character
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.2 – Bad character
text_marked:
Evidence of an offender’s bad character, i.e., their prior criminality,[^1277] is also relevant to a court in exercising the sentencing discretion, but it cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence[^1278] or to doubly punish an offender.[^1279] Instead, it may indicate an offender’s moral culpability, persistent lawlessness or a propensity to commit particular crimes and so inhibit consideration of mitigatory factors such as rehabilitation.[^1280]
The list of legislative considerations above is not exclusive: ‘previous findings of guilt or convictions’ does not refer only to those made or recorded prior to the commission of the offence currently before the court.[^1281] However, as with prior convictions, subsequent convictions cannot be used to increase the head sentence, but only to counter an inference that an offender’s later conduct was mitigating.[^1282]
Subsequent convictions recorded after the commission of the offence before the court are also relevant, but again cannot be considered to aggravate an offence and can only be considered for the purpose of rebutting alleged circumstances of mitigation.[^1283] The defence has no duty to inform the court of subsequent convictions, unless relying on the offender’s good character, but the prosecution has a duty to prove later convictions and other relevant subsequent conduct whenever it is open to the court to fix a non-parole period.[^1284] ‘Subsequent convictions’ are not proved through the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic) provisions on tendering an offender’s previous convictions. Instead, they may be placed before the court in the course of submissions.
Lastly, if there is evidence of rehabilitation subsequent to the offending and prior to sentencing, then bad character may have a reduced negative impact.[^1285]

title: Motive
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.2 – Motive
text_marked:
An offender’s motive may be considered in assessing their culpability.[^1286] It may be an aggravating or mitigating factor,[^1287] and the weight it is to be given depends on the circumstances.
Culpability may be lessened if the offending was motivated by:
• genuine altruism,[^1288] as opposed to ‘false’ altruism;[^1289]
• addiction linked to offending with no profit motive;[^1290]
• personal or financial pressures or need;[^1291] or
• threats falling short of the defence of duress.[^1292]
Culpability may be aggravated for offending motivated by:
• misguided loyalty;[^1293]
• greed or profit;[^1294]
• a desire for status, self-aggrandisement or to fund a lavish lifestyle;[^1295]
• vigilantism, the law does not condone revenge or an offender punishing the victim;[^1296] or
• revenge, spite, or dislike.[^1297]

title: Childhood
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood
text_marked:
Bugmy has made clear that an offender’s circumstances and experiences of deprivation or violence during their childhood and formative years must be considered in sentencing – not just out of historical curiosity but because the effects of social disadvantage do not diminish with time.[^1299] They are likely to have profound and lasting consequences that can explain, but not excuse, the offending. Taking lifelong damage that is the result of childhood exposure to violence, abuse, or neglect into account when sentencing is ‘the mark of a humane society….’[^1300] It is also relevant in applying the fundamental principles and sentencing purposes.[^1301]
It is not possible to identify every relevant and mitigating circumstance, but significant circumstances include being raised in an environment of, or being exposed or subjected to:
• family violence or abuse;[^1302]
• parents or caretakers who were addicts or alcoholics;[^1303]
• educational disadvantage;[^1304]
• sexual abuse;[^1305]
• separation from natural parents;[^1306] or,
• severe forms of persecution and violence, including witnessing death of family members, and time spent as a refugee.[^1307]
However, it is an error to require the offender to demonstrate ‘significant childhood deprivation’.[^1308] There is no requirement that the deprivation be “profound”.[^1309]
A court should make clear to what extent the offender’s background and history have moderated the weight given to one purpose or principle over another.[^1310] If any, for deprivation will not always ameliorate sentence, the court ‘must evaluate the extent to which past disadvantage has featured in the offender’s upbringing and impacted the course of their life’.[^1311]
While disadvantage will always remain relevant, at some point mitigation must yield in the face of serious violent offending and the need for community protection.[^1312] This is particularly so in cases of domestic violence; childhood disadvantage cannot mitigate a sentence, ‘such that victims of domestic violence… are treated as less worthy of protection or that the crimes against them warrant less denunciation’.[^1313]

title: Childhood
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood
text_marked:
But as with youth, a disadvantaged upbringing may elevate the importance of rehabilitation, and so of the need to avoid or minimise incarceration, as a sentencing consideration in order to end a cycle of offending that is of ‘great detriment to the community and of the applicant….’[^1314]
Lastly, it is important to distinguish the way in which deprivation is being considered and what must support that consideration. Bugmy said: 1) that an offender’s circumstances of childhood deprivation may mitigate their sentence because their moral culpability is likely to be less than one who was not so exposed, and 2) that an offender’s extreme deprivation may explain their recourse to violence when frustrated, to the extent that their moral culpability may be substantially reduced.[^1315] Hermann has characterised the first of these as being the “general expression” of the relevance of childhood deprivation, and the second as being the "specific expression".[^1316]
The Court of Appeal has further said that the general expression can be inferred from the simple fact of deprivation; there is no requirement to establish a causal connection between the background and the offending because a background of significant deprivation is likely to leave an indelible mark and so will generally lessen an offender’s culpability.[^1317]
However, the second expression requires a nexus between childhood deprivation and the inability to control an impulse relevant to the offending conduct before it can substantially reduce an offender’s culpability. It must be established that the childhood experience does explain the offending conduct, at least in part. There must be a causal connection, established by an appropriate evidentiary foundation.[^1318]
Further, careful consideration needs to be given to whether the evidence establishes the required nexus. There must be a ‘rigorous evaluation of the evidence’ and not a mechanical application which permits a diagnostic label to automatically invoke the specific application of Bugmy.

text_marked:
A disadvantaged background is not in itself sufficient to attract more than the general application of Bugmy. There must be a specific evidentiary foundation, which establishes and explains the relevant nexus, to invoke the specific application. The nexus cannot be inferred from judicial or other experience, or common sense. The evidence must be evaluated carefully,[^1319] and while an expert psychological or psychiatric report may not be required in every case, the Court has clearly stated that it is difficult to envision a case where the evidentiary basis for a specific application of the Bugmy principles will be sufficiently strong in the absence of a “professional reasoned opinion”.[^1320]
For detailed research relating to experiences of disadvantage and deprivation please see the Bugmy Bar Book.

title: Remorse
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse
text_marked:
Remorse is also referred to as ‘repentance’ or ‘contrition’ and is a relevant consideration at common law and a statutory consideration when sentencing for Commonwealth offences.[^1323] It is not directly identified as a relevant consideration under the Victorian regime, but the Act implicitly incorporates it as one by stating that a court may consider the effects of a forfeiture order or an offender’s conduct during trial or hearing as an indicator of remorse.[^1324]
Genuine remorse is extremely rare and a very important element of sentencing as it enhances the offender’s prospects of rehabilitation and reduces the need for specific deterrence and community protection. It may be demonstrated by making admissions to conduct that would otherwise have been difficult to prove or that provide the prosecution with evidence necessary to obtain a conviction, and when such a confession is made it warrants a ‘demonstrable discount’ in sentence in order to encourage similar admissions from other offenders.[^1325] This significantly mitigating factor is known in Victoria as the ‘Doran Discount’, and it has been held to apply further to admissions that lead to the laying of an increased number of charges or to more serious charges.[^1326] The discount is not confined to cases where the crime was unknown before the confession or where the complainant did not have capacity to give evidence. The discount may also be available where the offender made the confession after the offender was presented with the evidence against them, if that affected the form of the charge.[^1327] Depending on the admissions, a discount of 30% to 50% may be appropriate.[^1328] The discount will generally be more substantial when the confession is made to an unknown crime and less when it only provides detail of existing allegations. Nonetheless, if proof depends entirely on the confession, leniency is called for. The amount is a matter of degree and fact depending on the circumstances.[^1329]

title: Remorse
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse
text_marked:
An offender’s guilty plea made appreciating the wrongfulness of their conduct, its impact on the victim, and wishing to repair any harm out of a wish to clear their conscience also calls for an exercise of mercy in the form of a significant sentence reduction beyond that given to all guilty pleas for their utilitarian value.[^1330]
However, even genuine remorse cannot make up for some harms and it does not displace the need for the gravity of offending to be reflected in the sentence.[^1331]
Genuine remorse must be contrasted with feigned remorse, self-pity, or depression. The ‘anguish’ at being caught and punished is not an indication of remorse. An offender’s determination to change their behaviour and to make amends to the extent possible is.[^1332]
An offender who wants to rely on remorse in mitigation must ‘satisfy the court there is genuine penitence and contrition and a desire to atone’.[^1333] This must be established on proper evidence and a court should be cautious before accepting that an offender’s guilty plea indicates remorse warranting more than a utilitarian discount.[^1334] A court is also entitled to consider a lengthy period of delay between the offending and the guilty plea as detracting from the quality of the offender’s remorse and prospects for rehabilitation.[^1335]
The degree of an offender’s true remorse is a question of fact to be determined on the balance of probabilities.[^1336] The most ‘compelling evidence’ of remorse is the offender’s testimony and a court is not bound to accept other ‘second-hand evidence’. The words and deeds of the offender over time are ‘more informative and precise’.[^1337] Hardship to the offender and the willingness to assume significant burdens to make restitution is a strong indication of remorse.[^1338]
A victim impact statement cannot be used to disprove a claim of remorse. The prosecution will ordinarily need to lead admissible evidence in order to disprove a claim of remorse.[^1339]
In addition to the Doran Discount discussed above, remorse may be indicated by other conduct, including:
• confessing to the police sometime after the crime;[^1340]
• seeking treatment;[^1341]

title: Remorse
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse
text_marked:
• acting in a manner that saves the victim further distress;[^1342]
• making restitution;[^1343]
• cooperating with the police and authorities;[^1344]
• apologising to the victim;[^1345]
• facilitating the conduct of the trial or the administration of justice.[^1346]
Similarly, conduct may also qualify or indicate a lack of remorse, such as where an offender:
• attempts to deceive the court or exaggerates a mitigating factor to obtain a lesser sentence;[^1347]
• contests the mental elements of a crime;[^1348]
• lies in the face of charges or offers false alibis;[^1349]
• pleads largely in ‘recognition of the inevitable’, such as where the prosecution’s case is strong;[^1350]
• conceals the victim’s body and lies to cover up their involvement in the crime.[^1351]
The absence of remorse cannot be a circumstance of aggravation.[^1352] But it may indicate a need for specific deterrence.[^1353] If evidence establishing a lack of remorse reveals a contemptuous attitude to the victim or the law, it may also be relevant to the offender’s moral culpability and prospects for rehabilitation. Whether this is so will depend on the circumstances of the individual case.[^1354]
The genuineness of remorse and the time and manner it manifests should be evaluated in light of the overall facts.[^1355] Timing is relevant in that remorse is generally given less weight the later it appears.[^1356] But an offender’s remorse is not measured at the time of the offending.[^1357]

title: Restitution
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.2 – Restitution
text_marked:
If an offender repays or compensates a victim, this restitution is a statutorily required consideration in assessing remorse for Commonwealth offending,[^1358] but apart from that it is also a relevant factor at common law that allows for a sentence to be reduced or a shorter non-parole period to be fixed.[^1359] But even full reparation does not entitle an offender to avoid all aspects of punishment.[^1360]
The principles of restitution may be summarised as follows:
• it is always relevant and mitigating;[^1361]
• it should be encouraged;[^1362]
• it provides some reparation for the victim, indicates remorse, and means the offender has not profited from their crime;[^1363]
• hardship and the willingness to assume significant burdens to make restitution should be given great weight;[^1364]
• mitigation is not removed but may be lessened when restitution is made by third-parties or by court order;[^1365]
• a court should not permit an offender to buy, or appear to buy, a reduction in or suspension of their sentence;[^1366]
• offers of restitution made for the first time on plea are to be viewed cautiously;[^1367]
• there may be rare circumstances where it is appropriate for a court to defer sentencing to permit an offender a chance to make good on an offer of restitution, but requests to do so should be viewed cautiously;[^1368]
• differences in the amount of restitution made may explain disparate sentences;[^1369]
• failure to make full or partial restitution is not an aggravating factor.[^1370]

title: Benefits
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits
text_marked:
The value of an accused’s plea of guilty is recognised both by the common law and statute.
The Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’) requires a court to consider whether the offender pleaded guilty and at what stage in the proceedings any plea or intention to plead occurred.[^1371] Moreover, when an accused is being committed for trial, the magistrate must inform them that the sentencing court may consider any plea and the stage at which it is given.[^1372]
The courts have consistently acknowledged the public interest in an accused pleading guilty. A guilty plea saves the State and the victims the cost (human and financial), and trauma of a trial.[^1373] The economic advantage to the community when a person pleads guilty are the saving of judicial, prosecutorial and legal aid resources, witness fees, and the fees paid to (and the inconvenience experienced by) jurors.[^1374]
For witnesses and their families, particularly those in homicide and sexual offence cases, a guilty plea spares them from the ordeal of having to give evidence.[^1375] Pleas of guilty assist victims to put their experiences behind them, to receive vindication and support from their family and friends, and possibly to obtain assistance from the community for any injury they may have suffered.[^1376]
The other benefits of an accused person pleading guilty are relieved congestion in the courts, and improved finalisation rates for criminal cases with a consequent increase in public confidence in the criminal justice system.[^1377]
When an accused person offers their plea of guilty, they abandon any chance of being acquitted, even undeservedly.[^1378]

title: Benefits
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits
text_marked:
For these reasons, an accused person’s plea of guilty is publicly rewarded: the purpose being to encourage offenders to plead guilty[^1379] because of the significant public good that follows when they do. In particular, while Victorian courts work under the adverse effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, a sentencing court should ‘view a plea of guilty as carrying with it a greater utilitarian benefit than at other times, and in other circumstances, and, concomitantly, as attracting an augmented mitigatory effect on sentence, simply because the plea will benefit the beleaguered administration of justice’. Given the circumstances, courts must provide actual encouragement to relieve strains on the system by encouraging the accused to plead guilty. All other things being equal, a plea entered during the currency of the pandemic is worth greater weight in mitigation than a plea entered at a time when the community and the courts are not affected by the effects of the pandemic. It should attract a significant discount (which the court does not need to quantify)[^1380] but not one ‘with a malleable weight, dependent on Court venue….’[^1381] The discount for having pled during the pandemic must be applied consistently.[^1382]
It has been noted, however, that as at the end of 2023 the effects of the pandemic upon the criminal justice system in Victoria have subsided.[^1383]

title: Utilitarian benefit
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit
text_marked:
In all but exceptional cases, the utilitarian value of a plea must be acknowledged by a reduction in the sentence imposed.[^1386] This recognises the objective benefit to the community regardless of whether the plea is accompanied by any evidence of remorse or contrition.[^1387] Even a plea motivated by self-interest has a utilitarian benefit.[^1388]
The strength of the Crown case will have no bearing on the assessment of (and reward for) the utilitarian value of a guilty plea[^1389] because it does not bear upon the objective benefits of the plea.[^1390] But the length and complexity of any trial that has been rendered unnecessary by the guilty plea is relevant to the assessment of the utilitarian benefit.[^1391]
If the Crown must prove an overwhelmingly complex and lengthy circumstantial case, the benefit of a guilty plea might be considered great.[^1392]
When an accused pleads guilty to some charges but contests others, this does not diminish the weight to be attached to the utilitarian benefit of the pleas of guilty.[^1393]
While a plea of guilty must always be taken into account as a mitigating factor,[^1394] a plea of not guilty is never an aggravating factor. An accused person cannot be penalised for insisting on their right to trial, and a court may not mark its disapproval of the accused having put the issues to proof or having presented a time wasting or even scurrilous defence by increasing what is a proper sentence.[^1395]
Clearly there is a ‘certain illogicality’ between the principle of a guilty plea discount and the prohibition on treating a plea of not guilty as aggravating.[^1396] But the principles, however competitive, are entrenched and operate to restrain a wrongful approach to sentencing.[^1397]

While a plea of guilty must always be taken into account as a mitigating factor, a plea of not guilty is never an aggravating factor. An accused person cannot be penalised for insisting on their right to trial, and a court may not mark its disapproval of the accused having put the issues to proof or having presented a time wasting or even scurrilous defence by increasing what is a proper sentence. Clearly there is a ‘certain illogicality’ between the principle of a guilty plea discount and the prohibition on treating a plea of not guilty as aggravating. But the principles, however competitive, are entrenched and operate to restrain a wrongful approach to sentencing.

title: Indicator of remorse
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.2 – Indicator of remorse
text_marked:
A guilty plea that demonstrates genuine remorse, that is entered at the earliest practical opportunity, that saves the State a trial and witnesses both trauma and inconvenience normally deserves a substantial sentencing discount.[^1398]
The strength of the Crown case may be relevant when determining the degree to which a guilty plea reflects the offender’s remorse.[^1399] A strong Crown case may warrant a conclusion that the plea is merely the offender ‘recognising the inevitable’ and a finding that remorse, contrition and willingness to facilitate the course of justice are not indicated.[^1400] However, care should be taken before concluding that a plea of guilty to a strong Crown case indicates an absence of contrition because whatever the strength of the Crown case an offender may be genuinely remorseful and accepting of responsibility.[^1401] For guilty pleas where the Crown case is weak, an additional level of discount is generally warranted.[^1402]
Where remorse may be inferred from a guilty plea, a court should identify the weight it has attributed to the plea and how it was taken into account.[^1403]

title: Timing
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing
text_marked:
A plea given early and unconditionally should ordinarily attract a substantial sentencing discount.[^1404] A plea made at the earliest opportunity that evidences genuine remorse and prospects of rehabilitation, which saves the State a trial and witnesses trauma and inconvenience, normally justifies a high discount. An early plea that does nothing but save the costs of a trial usually still attracts a significant discount.[^1405]
A late plea attracts a discount, but it will generally be of lower value. How the timing of a guilty plea is characterised depends on the facts of the case and involves establishing the time it could first be said it was reasonably open to the offender to plead guilty.[^1406]
A guilty plea will not be late:
• when it is made to a lesser offence shortly after the prosecution discontinues a more serious charge; • when it is entered after the prosecution withdraws other charges, where the accused was reasonably avoiding forensic prejudice by withholding the plea until those other charges were withdrawn.[^1407] However, an accused does not act reasonably in delaying a guilty plea if the object or effect of the delay is to secure a forensic advantage or avoid a forensic disadvantage in relation to any other charged offences;[^1408]
• if the offender pleaded guilty to the offence of which they were ultimately convicted as soon as they were told that it was the only charge they would face;[^1409]
• where the offender pleads guilty as soon as a charge was amended to reflect the proper factual basis or particulars of the offending.[^1410]
However, where a statutory alternative is available, a shift in the factual basis of the allegation will not necessarily mean a later plea is recast as ‘early’ if the offender could have pleaded guilty to the alternative allegation at an earlier stage.[^1411]
Where a plea is late, and an accused has caused lengthy expensive extradition proceedings, the discount for the plea may be small.[^1412]

title: Imprisonment
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.1 – Imprisonment
text_marked:
Where a sentence of imprisonment is imposed, the discount is first applied to the head sentence as the prisoner must, hypothetically, serve every day of that sentence. Next, the discount is applied to the non-parole period. The plea may even incur an additional discount at this stage if it also evidences rehabilitative prospects.[^1417]
A mandatory minimum term of imprisonment can create complications for reductions in sentence for mitigatory factors, including pleas of guilty. A minimum sentencing regime does not oust common law sentencing principles but necessarily modifies both.[^1418] There is little authority available on the question of mitigation in the context of mandatory sentencing regimes; the issue is likely to arise more frequently as the number of offences subject to minimum sentencing requirements increases. There is some guidance from Western Australia.[^1419]

title: Gravity of offending
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.3 – Gravity of offending
text_marked:
There are competing authorities on the question of whether an offender pleading guilty to an offence in the ‘worst category’ of offending should be entitled to a discount for their plea. One line rejects the notion that a more serious offence is less likely to attract a plea discount. Those cases tend to focus on the utilitarian benefit of the plea and the fact that it spares victims (or their families) from the trauma of giving evidence. Reasoning in this way, the greater the seriousness of the crime, the greater the weight to be given to a plea of guilty.[^1421]
However, more recent authority considers whether the enormity of the offenders’ criminality is such that the utilitarian benefit of their guilty plea must yield to greater considerations such as the protection of the public and the maintenance of the rule of law.[^1422]
It is now generally held that for the worst instances of murder, the entry of a guilty plea is a necessary condition for the fixing of a non-parole period,[^1423] but it should not be assumed that a plea will save a murderer from life imprisonment.[^1424]

title: Section 6AAA notional sentence
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence
text_marked:
The common law holds that the justification for a sentence reduction must be transparent.[^1425] Further to that proposition, Parliament has legislated to advance the public interest in having offenders plead guilty by providing conspicuous rewards to those who do so.[^1426]
Specifically, section 6AAA of the Act requires a court, when imposing certain forms of sentence, to state the benefit the offender has received because of their guilty plea.[^1427]
The court must articulate a ‘notional sentence’ it would have imposed after trial if the offender had not pleaded guilty.
This obligation arises when the sentence involves:
• a custodial order; or
• an order that the offender serve a term of imprisonment; or
• a Community Corrections Order for a period of two years or more; or • a fine exceeding 10 penalty units; or
• an aggregate fine exceeding 20 penalty units.[^1428]
The notional sentence only needs to be stated if the court has imposed a less severe sentence because of the guilty plea.[^1429] It also only needs to be stated in relation to the overall sentence, not in relation to individual charges. If a total effective sentence is imposed in respect of multiple offences, the periods to be stated are the total effective sentence and single non-parole period, if any.[^1430]
Aggregate sentences are to be treated as a single sentence for the purposes of s 6AAA.[^1431]
If a non-parole period is imposed, the notional undiscounted non-parole period must also be stated.[^1432]
It is unclear what is expected of the s 6AAA statement when the offender has pleaded guilty to some but not all charges. The Court of Appeal has suggested the notional sentence is to be made regarding only the total effective sentence.[^1433]
In cases where a s 6AAA statement is not required because of the form of sentence being imposed, a court may still state the notional sentence that would have been imposed but for the offender’s plea of guilty.[^1434]

title: Obligation to record
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.1 – Obligation to record
text_marked:
Where the court states a notional sentence, it must record or cause it to be recorded (whether in writing or in another form) in the records of the court.[^1435]
Section 6AAA requires the court (at least privately) to isolate considerations flowing from the plea. However, it does not require the court to explain that allocation in the sentencing reasons. Judicial silence in this respect may be consistent with the doctrine of instinctive synthesis, and it may avoid some difficulties of unravelling interlinked considerations.
However, if a factor such as remorse has an important impact on sentence, it may be appropriate to indicate whether it has been treated as part of the general synthesis or as a consequence of the guilty plea. Sometimes, mitigating factors will continue to have force even after they are considered as part of the mitigation for the plea of guilty.[^1436] A failure to note an important factor affecting sentencing may erode the explanatory value of the statement of the notional post-trial sentence.

title: Aspects of the plea relevant to fixing
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.2 – Aspects of the plea relevant to fixing
text_marked:
The statement of the notional sentence requires the court, as a hypothetical exercise, to ignore the plea of guilty and determine the sentence that would have been imposed after a trial.[^1437] This exercise has been described as artificial and intellectually difficult.[^1438]
One aspect of the difficulty arises when the court considers what part of the plea should be quantified for the purposes of the sentence reduction. Can a plea of guilty be isolated from the remorse, admissions and acceptance of responsibility that attend it? Should the utilitarian value of the plea be isolated, for example, while other aspects of the plea such as the presence of remorse or an acceptance of responsibility are left out of this analysis? In Victoria, the preference is to take each aspect of the plea together to arrive at the reduction in sentence. On this approach, an offender who had made admissions, pleaded guilty, was remorseful and offered to assist authorities would have the combination of these considerations quantified for the purposes of the reduction in their sentence. Once such factors are considered as part of the reduction in sentence for the plea of guilty, that does not exhaust the mitigating effect of factors such as remorse and contrition. They continue to have independent force in the sentencing process.[^1439]

title: Methodology
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.3 – Methodology
text_marked:
The Court of Appeal has endorsed the following process:[^1440]
• determine the sentence that should be imposed by the instinctive synthesis; and • attempt to identify how much longer the sentence would have been had the offender not pleaded guilty.[^1441]
An alternative approach is to determine the notional sentence first and then determine the actual sentence by subtracting the benefit attributable to the guilty plea and its attendant considerations from that notional sentence. Ultimately the method is not governed by the Act or authority, and it remains a discretionary decision. However, courts should be cautious not to engage in two-tiered sentencing when applying s 6AAA. It is not permissible to take a starting point and then add or subtract periods of time representing aggravating or mitigating circumstances.[^1442]

title: Undertakings to cooperate
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.4 – Undertakings to cooperate
text_marked:
Past cooperation should be taken into account when declaring a notional sentence,[^1443] but different approaches have been taken where an offender has given undertakings as to future cooperation.[^1444]
Though perhaps ‘unrealistic’ and ‘artificial’ to assess future assistance for the purpose of stating the notional sentence, the process has some utility when resentencing an offender who failed to comply with their undertaking. Where the reduction for offering to co-operate and the other aspects of the guilty plea are dealt with compendiously, it would be inappropriate to increase the sentence by more than part of the discount allowed when resentencing the offender who failed to cooperate in accordance with their undertaking.[^1445]

title: Further difficulties
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.5 – Further difficulties
text_marked:
Sometimes a guilty plea has significance in an unusual way, making the statement of the notional sentence even more difficult. In Marannu v The Queen[^1446] the Court noted that the s 6AAA statement was particularly artificial in circumstances where it thought that a jury may not have convicted the appellant in all the circumstances of the case.[^1447]
In R v Mohamad[^1448] the Court noted that the notional sentence was difficult to apply because if he had not pleaded guilty, the offender would have faced more serious charges at trial.[^1449]
The hypothetical post-trial sentence was also the subject of comment in Samac v The Queen[^1450] when the Court noted the difficulty of declaring the hypothetical sentence after trial; sentencing facts cannot sensibly be presumed to coincide with the evidence led at the hypothetical trial, which resulted in the presumed guilty verdict.[^1451] The question of the facts that would have been found at the hypothetical trial also arises on appeal if the factual bases as found by the sentencing judge are successfully challenged on appeal and the appellant falls to be resentenced.[^1452]

title: Further difficulties
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.5 – Further difficulties
text_marked: In Mason (a pseudonym)[^1453] the Court observed that where both Sentencing Act 1991 s 6AAA and Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) s 16AC apply, it is not desirable to aggregate the discounts and specify the component attributable to both factors (plea of guilty and discount for future co-operation). Contrary to the approach encouraged in Couper,[^1454] the Court held that the process of attempting to assimilate the s 6AAA statement and the s 16AC specification is unnecessary and causes confusion. The two processes are better kept separate.[^1455] The judge should assess what they would have done in the absence of the undertaking and make the appropriate specification and separately identify what sentence would have been imposed if there had been no plea of guilty.[^1456] The Court did not, however, identify if the specification of the sentence that would have been imposed but for the undertaking assumes that the offender pleaded guilty or not guilty. The Court’s disapproval of the previous practice of specifying the aggregate ‘without discount’ sentence and then itemising the components of the discount suggests that the sentencing judge should assume a plea of not guilty. But as most offers to provide future co-operation occur in conjunction with a plea of guilty, any attempt to formulate a discount for co-operation in the absence of a plea of guilty is likely to be an especially artificial exercise.

title: Appellate issues
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.4 – Section 6AAA notional sentence > 7.1.4.6 – Appellate issues
text_marked:
The notional sentence is not a part of the sentence imposed, and errors or inadequacies in that figure are, in themselves, not appealable.
Section 6AAA does not identify any consequences for failing to specify the discount. However, the Act states generally that a court’s failure to give reasons or to comply with another procedural requirement of the Act does not invalidate any sentence it imposes.[^1457]
This likely applies to the s 6AAA requirement. Moreover, the Court of Appeal has noted that a failure to make the s 6AAA declaration is an irregularity and will ‘rarely, if ever, justify interfering with the sentence’ when sufficient weight has nonetheless been given to the plea of guilty.[^1458]
Ultimately, s 6AAA statements are based on an uncertain hypothesis[^1459] and sentencing courts synthesise a number of factors to arrive at an appropriate sentence. A plea of guilty is one of those factors.[^1460] Accordingly, it is not always helpful to simply consider any percentage discount given to determine whether sufficient weight was given to the guilty plea. Further, it may be that the sentencing court erred not in the actual sentence, but in the hypothetical sentence.[^1461]
Despite these observations, the Court of Appeal has used the s 6AAA statement (with other factors) to reason that the sentence imposed contained error. For example: the notional sentence may be relevant as a particular of a ground asserting the actual sentence was manifestly excessive or inadequate,[^1462] or in reasoning that insufficient weight was given to a guilty plea.[^1463] However, these cases will be rare.[^1464]

title: Sentence indication
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication
text_marked: The sentence indication schemes in the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic) (‘CPA’) are designed to put defendants who may ultimately plead guilty in a position to make this decision early in the proceedings.[^1465] The schemes allow for more authoritative advice to be given to the accused on the likely penalty to assist in making their plea decision earlier. There are some significant differences between the schemes in the Magistrates’ and the higher courts for sentencing indications. The procedural aspects will be dealt with separately here.

Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication
The sentence indication schemes in the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic) (‘CPA’) are designed to put defendants who may ultimately plead guilty in a position to make this decision early in the proceedings. The schemes allow for more authoritative advice to be given to the accused on the likely penalty to assist in making their plea decision earlier. There are some significant differences between the schemes in the Magistrates’ and the higher courts for sentencing indications. The procedural aspects will be dealt with separately here.

title: Magistrates’ Court
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.1 – Magistrates’ Court
text_marked:
A magistrate may give a sentence indication on their own initiative[^1466] at any time during a proceeding for a summary offence or an indictable offence that may be heard and determined summarily.[^1467]
However, a magistrate’s power to give a sentence indication is only engaged once summary jurisdiction has been invoked: the legislative purpose of the sentencing indication is not so broad as to encompass a sentence indication where the Magistrates’ Court had no power to deal with the charge.[^1468]
A magistrate may indicate which one of two results will follow if the accused pleads guilty to a particular charge at that time. These are either:
• the court would be likely to impose a sentence of imprisonment to be served immediately; or
• the court would be likely to impose a sentence of a specified type.[^1469]
While a magistrate may indicate a sentence of ‘a specified type’, this is limited to indicating the ‘type of sanction’ and does not permit indication of the quantum.
A magistrate who indicated that the sentence would likely be a sentence of a particular type must not impose a more severe type than was indicated. However, they may sentence to a less severe sanction than that indicated.[^1470]
If the accused receives a sentence indication but does not plead guilty at the first available opportunity, another magistrate must hear the matter unless all the parties agree otherwise.[^1471] A sentence indication only binds the magistrate who gives the indication. It does not bind the court on any hearing before a different judge or magistrate.[^1472]
The application for a sentence indication and its determination cannot be used as evidence against the accused.[^1473]

title: Higher courts
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.2 – Higher courts
text_marked:
A judge may give a sentence indication at any time after the filing of the indictment,[^1474] but only on an application of the accused with the consent of the prosecution.[^1475]
The Court of Appeal has cautioned against the use of informal sentencing indications made in the absence of a formal application by the accused and the other protections afforded by the CPA because of the risk the indication might be given prematurely on an uninformed basis and an accused may feel pressured into pleading guilty to offences which they intend to contest.[^1476]
The court may indicate which of two results will follow if the accused pleads guilty to a particular charge at that time. These are that the court would be likely to impose a sentence of a specified type, or a specified maximum total effective sentence.[^1477]
If the applicant for a sentence indication is already in custody, an indication that an immediate sentence of imprisonment will be imposed means, practically, that on sentencing, the offender will be actually imprisoned from the time of sentence and extending into the future.[^1478]
A court that gives a sentence indication must not impose a more severe sentence than the sentence type or maximum total effective sentence than was indicated.[^1479] But the court may sentence the offender to a less severe sentence type or maximum total effective sentence than stated in the sentence indication.[^1480]
A sentence indication only binds the judge who gives the indication. It does not bind the court on any hearing before a different judge.[^1481]

title: Discretionary considerations
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.2 – Sentence indication > 7.2.3 – Discretionary considerations
text_marked:
Both higher court judges and magistrates have discretion whether to give a sentence indication.[^1482] That decision is final and conclusive.[^1483] However, the discretion must be exercised judicially and must not consider any irrelevant consideration.[^1484] There is no appellate review of the decision to give or not give a sentencing indication, however judicial review is available.[^1485]
Sentencing courts will generally decline to give an indication where the decision turns upon material that is not yet before the court. The CPA explicitly states that the court may decline to give a sentence indication if it considers that there is insufficient information before the court that addresses the effect of an offence on any victim.[^1486] The specific reference to the impact on any victim does not mean the other mandatory considerations do not need to be considered at the sentence indication stage. Regarding the presence or absence of remorse as a sentencing consideration, in New South Wales it has been held that a guilty plea that follows a sentence indication may be given less weight in mitigation than a guilty plea that is an expression of remorse.[^1487]
However, reliance upon a sentence indication is not necessarily inconsistent with the existence of remorse. This is a question of fact to be determined in all the circumstances of the case.

title: Policy
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.1 – Policy
text_marked:
It is very much in the public interest that those who commit offences received every encouragement by the courts to inform upon their co-offenders;[^1488] the courts have long recognised the community interest in fostering ‘dishonour among thieves’.[^1489]
An offender who assists the authorities is entitled to have that assistance considered in mitigation of sentence. An aspect of this factor in mitigation is its public nature. Section 5(2AB) of the Act requires the court to announce it is imposing a less severe sentence and have the undertaking and its details noted in the record of the court.[^1490]
The courts’ role in fostering cooperation with authorities is capable of producing sentences much lower than those that would otherwise be expected. This is a price that society must be willing to pay.[^1491]
The discount varies according to the level of cooperation, its subjective significance, and the utility or potential utility of the assistance given.

title: Applying the discount
path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount
text_marked:
The discount to be applied will rise or fall according to both objective and subjective factors. The lowest level of cooperation is making admissions and entering a plea of guilty. At higher levels, cooperation may involve implicating co-offenders or providing other information of assistance to authorities and giving evidence in criminal proceedings. The highest-level discount is reserved for so-called ‘true informers’, who assist authorities proactively, acting as ‘undercover’ agents to provide information and evidence, commonly at greatly increased personal risk.[^1492]
The term ‘informer’s discount’ has been applied to both the ‘true informer’ and to the person who co-operates with authorities after participating in the offending and being charged.[^1493] But terminology is of little assistance: the focus should be on the nature of the assistance that an offender provides and the consequences for the offender of providing that assistance.
