Orders for the dismissal, discharge, and release of offenders are available for both Commonwealth and Victorian offences. These orders are the least punitive form of sentencing and so are generally reserved for less serious offences. For Victorian offences, a court may release an offender where a charge has been proved, by making the following orders: • dismissal without recording conviction; • discharge on conviction; • release on adjournment without conviction; or • release on adjournment following conviction, on the offender giving an undertaking with conditions attached. They may be made to: • provide for an offender’s rehabilitation by allowing their sentence to be served in the community; • take account of the trivial, technical or minor nature of the offence committed; • allow the offender to demonstrate remorse in a manner agreed to by the court; • allow for circumstances where it’s not appropriate to record a conviction; • allow for circumstances where it’s not appropriate to impose more than a nominal punishment; • allow for other extenuating or exceptional circumstances that justify the court showing mercy to an offender.

title: Dismissals
path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.1 – Dismissals
text_marked:
If a court finds a person guilty it may order dismissal of the charge without recording a conviction.[^2545] This is solely available as a non-conviction order; there is no alternative of dismissal with conviction.
The discretion to dismiss arises only when the court is satisfied that the charge is proved or made out on the evidence and that the plea was a proper one.[^2546] Moreover, the offence must be of such a nature that it can properly be characterised as ‘trifling’. The circumstances must clearly indicate that it would be manifestly unfair and unreasonable to penalise an offender and impose the stigma of a conviction.[^2547] This might include trivial offending[^2548] or where a conviction might disqualify the offender from their profession.[^2549]
Dismissals may also be granted where strong steps have been taken towards rehabilitation,[^2550] or where previous good character and post-offence conduct would make a conviction disproportionate to the crime.[^2551]
Although the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’) does not confer any power to attach conditions to a dismissal, a court may make a separate order for compensation or restitution.[^2552]
Once a charge has been dismissed, it is not possible for it to be revived, even where the finding was later impugned.[^2553]
Once a charge is dismissed without a finding of guilt, it cannot be taken as a conviction for any purpose except as provided in the Act.[^2554] However, the Act provides it has the same effect as if a conviction had been recorded for:
• appeals against sentence; • proceedings for variation or breach of sentence; • proceedings against the offender for a subsequent offence; and
• subsequent proceedings against the offender for the same offence.[^2555]

title: Discharge
path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.2 – Discharge
text_marked:
If a court finds a person guilty of an offence it may record a conviction and order they be discharged without further conditions being imposed.[^2556] This requires a finding of guilt and a conviction to be recorded before the court may discharge.
An unconditional discharge is sometimes appropriate where:
• the offence is one of low culpability;[^2557]
• where minor conduct is subsumed in a more serious offence;[^2558] or
• there are compelling personal circumstances,[^2559] such as if financial circumstances preclude a fine,[^2560] or to allow rehabilitation and treatment to continue.[^2561]
However, where the offence was a serious one, the court may decide to impose a higher sentence than an unconditional discharge to denounce the conduct, notwithstanding other mitigating factors.[^2562]
Again, the Act does not confer any power to attach conditions to a discharge, but a court may make a separate order for compensation or restitution.[^2563]

path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.3 – Release on adjournment
text_marked:
Where a person has been found guilty of an offence, the court may adjourn the hearing and release the offender on an undertaking with conditions (‘adjourned undertaking’). This may be with or without recording a conviction.[^2564]
An adjourned undertaking is considered a ‘sentence’ despite not having a custodial component, and an offender is serving a sentence when placed on such an order.[^2565]

title: Imposing the order
path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.3 – Release on adjournment > 13.3.1 – Imposing the order
text_marked:
An order for an adjourned undertaking requires the court to be satisfied of the offender’s guilt[^2566] and it must have regard to the:
• nature of the offence; • character and past history of the offender; and
• impact recording a conviction will have on the offender's economic or social wellbeing or their employment prospects.[^2567]
This must also be balanced with the need for general deterrence.[^2568]
Before pronouncing sentence, the court should expressly indicate whether the accused is convicted or not.[^2569]
In addition to adjourning on an undertaking, a court may make an order for compensation or restitution.[^2570] Additional orders may also be imposed by operation of other legislation, such as license suspensions[^2571] and compulsory accredited driver education programs.[^2572]

title: Undertaking and length of order
path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.3 – Release on adjournment > 13.3.2 – Undertaking and length of order
text_marked:
The offender must first agree to give an undertaking before this sentencing option can be used and an agreement obtained just because imprisonment is a realistic alternative does not vitiate the consent.[^2573]
If a court places an offender on an adjourned undertaking, it must have the following conditions attached. That the offender:
• attend court if called on to do so and at the time to which the further hearing is adjourned (if specified);[^2574]
• be of good behaviour during the duration; and
• observe any special conditions imposed by the court.
Special conditions may include requiring the offender to make a payment directly to an organisation that provides a charitable or community service, or to the court through the Court Fund for payment to such an organisation.[^2575] If payment is made to the court, the court may choose the organisation at a later date.[^2576]
The court may also attach a justice plan condition, which will last for either the length of the adjournment or two years, whichever is shorter.[^2577]
The maximum duration of adjournment is five years (60 months).

title: Special conditions
path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.3 – Release on adjournment > 13.3.3 – Special conditions
text_marked:
As the Act does not define special conditions, it is open for the court to impose whatever condition it considers fit. Examples might include placing an offender under the care and direction of psychiatric clinicians,[^2578] a firearm prohibition,[^2579] non-contact conditions,[^2580] or special conditions as specified in other legislation, including:
• completing an approved drug education and information program per the Drugs, Poisons & Controlled Substances Act 1981 (Vic) s 76;[^2581] or
• completing an accredited driver education program[^2582] and a first-stage behaviour change program.[^2583]
A court should be cautious about imposing special conditions on leaving Victoria, residing out of Victoria, or any condition that might amount to an unauthorised deportation order.[^2584] Consideration should also be given to the appropriateness of an offender being simultaneously subjected to special conditions and to parole. title: Exercise of discretion to make order
path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.3 – Release on adjournment > 13.3.4 – Exercise of discretion to make order
text_marked:
An adjourned undertaking is usually made for minor offences.[^2585] However, it should not be made if doing so would breach the fundamental principles or sentencing purposes.[^2586]
An adjourned undertaking may be imposed for serious offences in exceptional circumstances. Instances include marginally excessive self-defence in the context of family violence,[^2587] serious psychiatric illness,[^2588] wellbeing of children or a partner as their carer,[^2589] possession of child pornography material in unusual circumstances,[^2590] or assistance to authorities.[^2591]
Other mitigating factors may also cause an adjourned undertaking to be imposed, such as significant delay,[^2592] the challenging environment of operation for a corporate offender,[^2593] the presence of an intellectual disability or mental health issue,[^2594] the offender’s youth or advanced age,[^2595] being an unwilling accomplice,[^2596] or time spent in immigration detention.[^2597]

title: Variation/Cancellation/Contravention of order
path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.3 – Release on adjournment > 13.3.6 – Variation/Cancellation/Contravention of order
text_marked:
The court may vary or cancel an adjourned undertaking on application at any time while the order is in force. The court must be satisfied that either:
• the offender’s circumstances have materially altered since the order was made and as a result the offender will not be able to comply with any condition of the undertaking; • the offender’s circumstances were wrongly stated or not accurately presented to the court or the author of a presentence report before the order was made; or
• the offender is no longer willing to comply with the conditions of the undertaking.[^2600]
The court must also consider the extent of the offender’s compliance with the order.[^2601]
If the court is so satisfied, it may vary or cancel the order and deal with the offender for the original offences as if it had just found them guilty of that offending. If a person is unable to comply with conditions, the court may impose a new adjourned undertaking without any conditions.[^2602]
If an offender contravenes the order without reasonable excuse, they may be liable for a maximum level 10 fine and having the order varied or cancelled.[^2603] If a court finds a person guilty of contravening an adjournment order, it must, in addition to sentencing the offender for that offence:
• vary the order as if an application was made to do so;
• confirm the order originally made;
• cancel the order (if it is still in force) and deal with the offender for the original offence as if it had just found them guilty of that offence; or • make no further order with respect to the offence in respect of which the original order was made.[^2604]
In determining how to deal with the offender a court must take account of the extent to which the offender has complied with the order, and their ability to comply.[^2605]
Variation or cancellation proceedings are commenced by application to the original sentencing court by:
• the offender;
• the DPP; • an informant in the original sentencing proceeding; • a member of the police force; or

path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.3 – Release on adjournment > 13.3.6 – Variation/Cancellation/Contravention of order
text_marked:
• an OPP lawyer. Notice of an application must be given to the offender, the DPP, and the informant or police prosecutor, depending on the circumstances.[^2606] The court may order that an arrest warrant be issued if the offender does not attend the hearing of the application.[^2607]
For contravention proceedings, if the original adjournment order was made in the Magistrates’ Court, proceedings are commenced by filing a charge sheet in that court. A charge sheet may be filed by: • the DPP; • the Chief Commissioner of Police;
• a member of the police force; • an informant in the original sentencing proceeding; • a Crown prosecutor; • a Regional Manager; • a community corrections officer; or • the Secretary to the Department of Justice.[^2608]
A proceeding must be brought in accordance with the provisions of, and rules and regulations made under, the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic) (‘CPA’), the Bail Act 1977
(Vic), and the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 (Vic), with any necessary modifications.[^2609]
For contraventions where the offender committed an offence punishable by imprisonment during the operation of the adjournment order, the proceeding must commence within six months of the conviction or finding of guilt for the later offence[^2610] and no more than two years after the adjournment order ceases to be in force.[^2611] For all other contraventions the proceeding must commence within one year of the adjournment order ceasing to be in force.[^2612]
If a charge sheet is filed in the Magistrates’ Court, but that court did not make the order that is the subject of the offence, it must transfer the proceeding to the appropriate sentencing court.[^2613] If this occurs, the Supreme or County Courts may hear and determine the proceeding under Chapter 3 of the CPA.[^2614]
If the original adjournment order was made in the Supreme or County Courts, and the offender has been convicted or found guilty of an offence that also contravened the adjournment order, the proceeding must be commenced by filing a charge sheet in the relevant sentencing court.[^2615]

title: Residential treatment orders
path: Part C – Sanctions > 14 – Residential treatment orders
text_marked:
A court may make a Residential Treatment Order (‘RTO’) directing that an offender be detained for up to five years in a residential treatment facility (‘RTF’) to receive specified treatment.[^2618]
An RTO is designed to detain and treat people with an intellectual disability who have committed serious sexual or other violent offences.[^2619] The intent is to ‘reduce the likelihood of re-offending by increasing the person’s ability to self-regulate and manage the[ir] offence-specific and related thoughts and behaviours with the ultimate aim of living in a less restrictive environment’.[^2620]
Since an RTO requires detention and treatment for a specified period, it should not be imposed if a less restrictive sanction is more suitable.[^2621]
An intention to impose an RTO may constitute ‘special reasons’ for not imposing a mandatory imprisonment term or a mandatory minimum term.[^2622]
An RTO may be ordered where the offender has been found guilty of sexual assault,[^2623] sexual assault by compelling sexual touching,[^2624] or a serious offence, which includes:
• murder, manslaughter, or child homicide;[^2625]
• causing serious injury offences;[^2626]
• threats to kill;[^2627]
• rape, rape by compelling sexual penetration, and assault with intent to commit a sexual offence;[^2628]
• sexual penetration offences occurring within a familial context;[^2629]
• sexual abuse or penetration of a child under 16;[^2630]
• kidnapping and abduction for sexual purpose offences;[^2631]
• armed robbery;[^2632]
• repealed equivalents of these listed offences;[^2633] or
• conspiracy, incitement, or attempting to commit any of these offences.[^2634]
Where an offender faces multiple charges, some of which are eligible for an RTO, the eligible offences cannot be used as a gateway to impose an RTO on all offences on the indictment. Separate sanctions that do not interfere with the RTO will need to be imposed for ineligible offences.[^2635]

title: Residential treatment orders
path: Part C – Sanctions > 14 – Residential treatment orders
text_marked:
If an offender faces multiple eligible charges, a single RTO may be imposed where all the offences are of the same kind and the same treatment program will be relevant. While a court may impose separate RTOs in respect of different charges, there is no power under the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) to order cumulation in respect of separate RTOs, and so the additional orders will be redundant.[^2636]
A court considering making an RTO may request:
• a pre-sentence report;[^2637]
• a statement from the Secretary to the Department of Human Services (‘DHS Secretary’) that the person has an intellectual disability;[^2638] and
• a plan of available services.[^2639]
The pre-sentence report will list the services or treatment specific to the offender that may assist them during the RTO.[^2640] A plan of available services lists the facilities and treatment programs available at the RTF and may be either generic[^2641] or detailed and specific to the offender’s circumstances.[^2642]
An RTO may only be ordered if the DHS Secretary has specified:
• the offender is suitable for admission to a RTF; and
• the services identified in the plan of available services are available at the RTF.[^2643]
If a court does make an RTO, it must provide the DHS Secretary with a copy.[^2644]
There is little specific guidance on fixing the length of an RTO, but it is a sentence and so must not be more severe than necessary to achieve its purposes.[^2645] However, depending upon the circumstances of the offence and the offender, it may be open for the court to make an RTO that exceeds the minimum period recommended in a pre-sentence report. The court is not required to determine the duration of the order by what would have been the appropriate length of imprisonment, so long as the RTO is proportionate to the offending conduct.[^2646]

title: Residential treatment orders
path: Part C – Sanctions > 14 – Residential treatment orders
text_marked:
An offender or the DHS Secretary may apply to the court for ‘extended leave’ from detention to enable the offender to be reintegrated within the community.[^2647] Before granting the application, the court must be satisfied on reasonable grounds that the safety of the offender or the public will not be seriously endangered as a result.[^2648]
Applications can be made and granted more than once,[^2649] and are for a maximum of 12 months and subject to any conditions imposed by the court.[^2650] The availability of extended leave may form part of the offender’s treatment in a pre-sentence report and may be a factor in ordering an RTO.[^2651]
Upon application,[^2652] the court that made the RTO may confirm, vary or cancel it if satisfied that:
• the offender is not complying with the order;[^2653]
• the offender’s needs are not being met by the order; or
• the order is no longer appropriate.[^2654]
An offender’s needs may not be met if the court determines a more restrictive environment, such as prison, will be more effective.[^2655] The court should also consider the need to protect the staff and other residents, or if any changes to the offender’s course of treatment has too great an impact on the RTF’s usual operations.[^2656]
If the court cancels the order, it may then deal with the offender as if they had just been found guilty of the offence(s).[^2657] If relevant, a new s 6AAA declaration must be made.[^2658]
In determining how to deal with an offender after cancelling an RTO, a court must consider the extent of the offender’s compliance with the order,[^2659] including whether the non-compliance was wilful or due to the offender’s complex needs.[^2660] The court may also adjourn sentence to assess the offender’s progress in a new environment for a new pre-sentence report.[^2661]
Pre-sentence detention cannot be declared for the RTO-imposed offence if it has already been declared for other offences dealt with at the time, although it may be considered generally.[^2662]

title: Court assessment and secure treatment orders
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders
text_marked:
A court can make orders for the involuntary assessment, treatment or detention of mentally ill offenders.
Two kinds of orders can be made under the Victorian regime: court assessment orders[^2663] and court secure treatment orders.[^2664] These are governed by Part 5 of the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’) and the Mental Health Act 2014 (Vic) (‘Mental Health Act’).[^2665] There are also two orders for Commonwealth offenders: hospital orders and psychiatric probation orders.[^2666] For more on these, please see the Commonwealth Sentencing Database.[^2667]
Prior to the Mental Health Act, the Act gave a court the power to make four different involuntary orders: assessment orders, diagnosis, assessment and treatment (‘DAT’) orders, restricted involuntary treatment orders, and hospital treatment orders. These four species of orders have essentially been replaced with the two kinds of order now available. Court assessment orders effectively replace DAT orders and assessment orders, and court secure treatment orders replace hospital treatment orders. Restricted involuntary treatment orders are now inpatient treatment orders.[^2668]
A court can only make a court assessment order or a court secure treatment order if ‘no less restrictive means’ are reasonably available to enable the person to be assessed or treated.[^2669] The inquiry into whether a less restrictive means is reasonably available will likely involve consideration of whether the patient can receive voluntary mental health treatment.[^2670]
The Mental Health Act operates on a presumption that people have the capacity to give informed consent to mental health assessment and treatment.[^2671]

title: Mental illness
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.1 – Mental illness
text_marked:
Orders under the Act can only be made if, among other requirements, the court is satisfied that the offender ‘appears to have a mental illness’ (in the case of a court assessment order) or in fact has a mental illness (in the case of a court secure treatment order). In Victoria, ‘mental illness’ is a medical condition that is characterised by a significant disturbance of thought, mood, perception or memory.[^2672] A person is not considered to have a mental illness only because they:
• express, refuse, or fail to express a particular political opinion or belief; • express, refuse, or fail to express a particular religious opinion or belief; • express, refuse, or fail to express a particular philosophy; • express, refuse, or fail to express a particular sexual preference, gender identity or sexual orientation; • engage in, refuse, or fail to engage in a particular political activity; • engage in, refuse, or fail to engage in a particular religious activity; • engage in sexual promiscuity; • engage in immoral conduct; • engage in illegal conduct; • engage in antisocial behaviour; • are intellectually disabled; • use drugs or consume alcohol; • have a particular economic or social status or are a member of a particular cultural or racial group; • are or have previously been involved in family conflict; • have previously been treated for mental illness.[^2673]
While the consumption of drugs or alcohol is not sufficient to assess a person as mentally ill, the serious temporary or permanent physiological, biochemical or psychological effects of such consumption may be regarded as an indication that a person has a mental illness.[^2674]
For the purposes of making a court assessment order or a court secure treatment order, the court does not need to be satisfied that the offender’s mental illness was a cause of the offending. It is only necessary that the offender be assessed as mentally ill at the time of sentencing, and that the other requirements for the orders are met.[^2675]

title: Designated mental health service
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.2 – Designated mental health service
text_marked:
The provisions of the Act dealing with court assessment orders and court secure treatment orders, refer to examination[^2676] and treatment occurring at a ‘designated mental health service’.[^2677]
A ‘designated mental health service’ means:[^2678]
• a prescribed public hospital;[^2679]
• a prescribed public health service;[^2680]
• a prescribed denominational hospital;[^2681]
• a prescribed privately-operated hospital;[^2682]
• a prescribed private hospital that is registered as a health service establishment;[^2683] or • the Victorian Institute of Forensic Mental Health.[^2684]

title: Court assessment orders
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.3 – Court assessment orders
text_marked:
There are two types of court assessment order:
• a community assessment order that a person be examined by an authorised psychiatrist in the community;[^2685] or
• an inpatient court assessment order that a person be taken to, and detained at, a designated mental health service and examined by an authorised psychiatrist.[^2686]
The order must state whether it is a community court assessment order or an inpatient court assessment order.[^2687]
Regardless of where the examination occurs, its purpose is to determine whether the person should be subject to either a temporary treatment order,[^2688] or a court secure treatment order.[^2689]

title: Required criteria
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.3 – Court assessment orders > 15.3.1 – Required criteria
text_marked:
The court may make a court assessment order if:
• on the trial or hearing of a person, the person is found guilty or pleads guilty;[^2690]
• the person is not in custody pending sentencing;[^2691]
• the person appears to have a mental illness;[^2692]
• due to the appearance of mental illness, the person appears to need immediate treatment to prevent: • serious deterioration in the person’s mental or physical health; or
• serious harm to the person or another person;[^2693]
• if an order is made, the person can be assessed;[^2694]
• there is no less restrictive means reasonably available to enable the person to be assessed;[^2695]
• a report has been received from an authorised psychiatrist for the designated mental health service where a person is to be assessed stating there are facilities and services available for such assessment;[^2696] and
• in the case of an inpatient court assessment order – the assessment cannot otherwise occur in the community.[^2697]

title: Additional requirements, duration, and powers
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.3 – Court assessment orders > 15.3.2 – Additional requirements, duration, and powers
text_marked:
After making an assessment order, a court must notify the authorised psychiatrist that the order has been made and provide them with a copy.[^2698]
If an inpatient court assessment order is made, the person must be taken to a designated mental health service as soon as practicable after it is made.[^2699]
A community assessment order comes into force when it is made and remains in force for seven days (for an inpatient court assessment order, the order expires seven days after the person is received at a designated mental health service).[^2700]
The authorised psychiatrist may vary a community assessment order to an inpatient court assessment order, or vice versa.[^2701]
If the court has considered a report made by an authorised psychiatrist after examining a person subject to a court assessment order, the court may:[^2702]
• make a court secure treatment order; or
• impose sentence according to law. Either way, the court must deduct any period of detention under the court assessment order from the duration of the sentence or court secure treatment order.[^2703]

title: Court secure treatment orders
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.4 – Court secure treatment orders
text_marked:
A court secure treatment order is a sentencing order that enables a person to be compulsorily detained and treated at a designated mental health service.[^2704] It is imposed on conviction.[^2705]
A hospital security order, the predecessor to a court secure treatment order, has been the subject of some judicial consideration[^2706] and given similarities between the two provisions, it is likely the analyses still largely apply.
Hospital security orders were made ‘by way of sentence’ but were not said to amount to a sentence of imprisonment.[^2707] However, a person subject to such an order was not excused from responsibility. They were not detained because they were mentally ill – they were detained because they had committed a serious offence.[^2708]
A court secure treatment order is a distinct sentencing option. A court that wishes to order a period of custody in an approved mental health service must make a court secure treatment order and may not impose a sentence of imprisonment with a direction on how it shall be served.[^2709]

title: Required criteria
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.4 – Court secure treatment orders > 15.4.1 – Required criteria
text_marked:
The court may make a court secure treatment order for a person who has been found guilty or pleads guilty, subject to several mandatory considerations.[^2710]
The first is that but for the person having a mental illness, the court would have sentenced them to a term of imprisonment.[^2711]
Second, the court is to consider the person’s current mental condition, physical and mental health, forensic history, and social circumstances.[^2712]
Third, the person must be examined by a psychiatrist and the court must be satisfied by the psychiatrist’s report (and any other evidence) that:
• the person has a mental illness; • because of this, they need treatment to prevent: • serious deterioration in their mental or physical health; or
• serious harm to themselves or another person; • the treatment will be provided if they are made subject to an order; and
• there is no less restrictive means reasonably available to receive the treatment.[^2713]
The requirement that a person ‘has a mental illness’ is different than for a hospital security order, which only requires the court to be satisfied that the person ‘appears to be mentally ill’. The change is consistent with the higher bar for involuntary treatment orders set by the Mental Health Act.
Finally, a court may only make a court secure treatment order after receiving a report from the authorised psychiatrist of the designated mental health service where it is proposed to treat the person. The report must recommend the making of the order, and state that there are facilities or services available at that service for the treatment of the person.[^2714]

title: Duration and effect as a term of imprisonment
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.4 – Court secure treatment orders > 15.4.2 – Duration and effect as a term of imprisonment
text_marked:
The duration of the order must not exceed the period of imprisonment that would have been ordered if the court had not made a court secure treatment order.[^2715] Thus, a court must consider what would otherwise have been the appropriate period of incarceration.[^2716]
If the offender is discharged from a court secure treatment order, the order has effect as a sentence of imprisonment for its unexpired period. That period must be served in prison unless the offender is released on parole.[^2717] The potential effect of this is that an offender subject to a court secure treatment order may be required to serve some, or virtually all, of the period in prison.[^2718]
Because a court secure treatment order is a sentencing order, the court must take into account all relevant sentencing considerations, in addition to the statutory criteria.[^2719]
An order for detention for the remainder of the offender’s life may be imposed for offences punishable by life imprisonment, as a life term is a sentence of a ‘specified duration’.[^2720]
When making a court secure treatment order, the court must fix a non-parole period as if it were a term of imprisonment.[^2721]

title: Aggregate court secure treatment order/multiple sanctions
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.4 – Court secure treatment orders > 15.4.3 – Aggregate court secure treatment order/multiple sanctions
text_marked:
A court may impose a single court secure treatment order in respect of multiple offences.[^2722] This power is available as a matter of statutory interpretation of the provisions allowing for court secure treatment orders and does not depend on the power to impose an aggregate sentence.[^2723]
The single order must not be longer than the appropriate period of imprisonment. A sentencing judge who imposes a single court secure treatment order must consider the otherwise appropriate dispositions for the individual offences and any cumulation orders. The totality principle applies to both the operational period of the order and non-parole period.[^2724]
It has been held that the court should specify the individual sentences that provide the basis for the court secure treatment order. This has been considered part of the obligation to provide adequate reasons.[^2725] While the obligation to give reasons has been limited by statute in relation to aggregate sentences of imprisonment,[^2726] there are no corresponding provisions relating to court secure treatment orders. It may be inappropriate to impose multiple court secure treatment orders.[^2727]
A court sentencing an offender for multiple offences may impose different penalties for the different offences, provided all orders can be given effect.[^2728]
text: A court may impose a single court secure treatment order in respect of multiple offences. This power is available as a matter of statutory interpretation of the provisions allowing for court secure treatment orders and does not depend on the power to impose an aggregate sentence. The single order must not be longer than the appropriate period of imprisonment. A sentencing judge who imposes a single court secure treatment order must consider the otherwise appropriate dispositions for the individual offences and any cumulation orders. The totality principle applies to both the operational period of the order and non-parole period. It has been held that the court should specify the individual sentences that provide the basis for the court secure treatment order. This has been considered part of the obligation to provide adequate reasons. While the obligation to give reasons has been limited by statute in relation to aggregate sentences of imprisonment, there are no corresponding provisions relating to court secure treatment orders. It may be inappropriate to impose multiple court secure treatment orders. A court sentencing an offender for multiple offences may impose different penalties for the different offences, provided all orders can be given effect.

title: Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders
text_marked:
A Drug and Alcohol Treatment Order (‘DATO’)[^2731] can only be made by the Drug Court Division of the Magistrates’ Court or County Court.[^2732]
Section 4B of the Magistrates Court Act 1989 (Vic) provides a mechanism for the transfer of a criminal matter to the Drug Court at any time before the formal plea. Before a proceeding is transferred, the Magistrates’ Court must be satisfied that the accused may be eligible for a DATO if convicted. This is a preliminary and limited enquiry. The referring Magistrate is not required to determine whether a DATO is appropriate, viable or a reasonably open sentencing option, nor are they to undertake a sentencing assessment. The Magistrate’s function is to determine whether the accused satisfies the eligibility requirements[^2733] for consideration by the Drug Court or whether any objective disqualification applies. But the ultimate assessment of whether a DATO is appropriate in all of the circumstances is for the Drug Court.[^2734]A DATO consists of a treatment and supervision part and a custodial part.[^2735] However, the offender does not serve the custodial part unless the Drug Court activates that part of the DATO.[^2736]
The purposes of a DATO include facilitating an offender’s recovery through judicially supervised therapeutic and integrated rehabilitation, protecting the community from further substance-driven offending and reducing the health risks associated with drug or alcohol dependence.[^2737] When considering whether to impose a DATO the Drug Court must regard rehabilitation and protection of the community, as achieved through the offender’s rehabilitation, as having greater importance than the other sentencing purposes.[^2738]

title: Custodial part
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.1 – Structure of the DATO > 15A.1.1 – Custodial part
text_marked:
The court must sentence the offender to a term of imprisonment which constitutes the custodial part of the DATO.[^2739] Its duration must be the length the court would have imposed if it had not made a DATO.[^2740] Once the sentence is imposed, it is automatically suspended. The offender will not serve that sentence unless it is subsequently activated.[^2741]
The maximum length of the custodial part depends on the jurisdiction:
• no more than 2 years in the Magistrates’ Court[^2742]
• no more than 4 years in the County Court.[^2743]
When setting the custodial part, the court must not set a non-parole period.[^2744] However, if the court activates the custodial part of the DATO for one year or more, the court may impose a non-parole period on the activated custodial part in accordance with the usual provisions of the Act.[^2745]
In determining the length of the custodial part, the court must not impose a longer sentence merely to allow the offender to be treated. This is both impermissible as a matter of law, and likely ineffective because program conditions only operate for 2 years, regardless of the length of the custodial part.[^2746]
Declaration of pre-sentence detention
The DATO incorporates a formal sentence of imprisonment[^2747] and so attracts the operation of s 18, which governs the declaration and deduction of pre-sentence detention for terms of imprisonment. The calculations for determining the maximum custodial period that may be activated, as set out in s 18ZE, rely upon formal declarations of pre-sentence detention.[^2748] The activation of a custodial part of a DATO, including activation following cancellation of the treatment and supervision part under ss 18ZN(1) or 18ZP(2)(a), does not constitute the imposition of a fresh sentence of imprisonment, and so does not provide a formal occasion for a s 18 declaration. It follows that, while practices have varied, it will generally be prudent for courts to declare any eligible custody at the time of imposing a DATO and not reserve this function for the time of activation of the custodial part.

title: Treatment and supervision part
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.1 – Structure of the DATO > 15A.1.2 – Treatment and supervision part
text_marked:
The treatment and supervision part of a DATO consists of mandatory core conditions that apply to all DATOs, and at least one program condition.[^2749] Any condition imposed under the treatment and supervision part of the DATO continues to operate for the duration of that specific part unless it is cancelled earlier.[^2750]
The Drug Court may vary the treatment and supervision part of a DATO if it considers it appropriate to do so based on its assessment of the offender’s progress.[^2751] Core conditions
The core treatment and supervision conditions must operate for either two years or the length of the custodial part, whichever is longer.[^2752]
The core conditions that apply to all DATOs are that an offender must:
• not re-offend by committing another offence punishable by imprisonment[^2753]
• attend Drug Court when required[^2754]
• report to a specified community corrections centre or another specified place within two clear workings days of the order being made[^2755]
• undergo treatment for drug or alcohol dependency as specified in the order, by the Drug Court, a specified community corrections officer, or a specified Drug Court officer[^2756]
• report to and accept visits from a specified community corrections officer or a specified Drug Court officer[^2757]
• give notice of any change of address within two clear working days of the change[^2758]
• not leave Victoria without permission,[^2759] and
• obey all lawful instructions and directions of the Drug Court, community corrections officers or specified Drug Court officers.[^2760]
Program conditions
The tailored program conditions attached to a DATO must operate for two years, regardless of the length of the custodial part.[^2761]
In making a DATO the Drug Court must attach at least one program condition,[^2762] but must not impose any more program conditions than necessary to achieve the purposes of the order.[^2763]
The program conditions that may be attached to a DATO are:
• compliance with drug or alcohol testing as directed[^2764]
• attendance at specified detoxification or other treatment (regardless of whether it is residential in nature)[^2765]
• attendance at specified vocational, educational, employment or other programs[^2766]

title: Case conferences
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.2 – Sanctions, rewards, activation, and cancellation > 15A.2.1 – Case conferences
text_marked:
The Drug Court may convene a case conference to be informed about an offender’s progress under a DATO. The case conference may include the offender’s lawyer, a prosecutor, a health service provider, a community correction officer or anyone else the judicial officer thinks appropriate.[^2771]
The Drug Court can vary the order on its own initiative or on the application of the offender, informant, police prosecutor, prosecutor, or certain prescribed persons. Variations may include:
• adding or removing program conditions; or
• varying one or more of the core conditions (other than the condition not to re-offend) or program conditions, by frequency of treatment or program, type of program, or degree of supervision.

title: Non-compliance ‘sanctions’
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.2 – Sanctions, rewards, activation, and cancellation > 15A.2.2 – Non-compliance ‘sanctions’
text_marked:
It is not an offence to breach or contravene a DATO. However, non-compliance with a DATO condition may result in the imposition by the court of sanctions.[^2772]
Where satisfied on the balance of probabilities that an offender has, without reasonable excuse, failed to comply with DATO conditions (other than by committing an offence punishable on conviction by imprisonment for more than 12 months), the Drug Court must consider the following sanctions in order and take only the first action it deems appropriate:
• confirm the treatment and supervision part of the DATO
• vary the treatment and supervision part of the order by adding or removing program conditions or by increasing the frequency of treatment or drug testing, or the degree of supervision
• make a curfew order
• order that the offender perform up to 20 hours of unpaid community work
• order that the offender remain at a specified place, other than a secure custody facility, for a specified period of up to 14 days, or
• if satisfied beyond reasonable doubt, that the offender has failed to comply with the condition attached to the DATO, order that the custodial part is activated for a specified period between one and seven days to be served in a secure custody facility.[^2773]
If satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that an offender has failed to comply with a condition on the order by committing an offence punishable on conviction by more than 12 months imprisonment, the Drug Court must either:
• impose any of the sanctions listed at (a)-(f) above as though the offender had failed to comply with any other attached condition,[^2774] or
• cancel the treatment and supervision part of the order,[^2775] after considering the extent to which the offender complied with the order and either:
• make an order activating some or all of the custodial part of the DATO,[^2776] or
• cancel the custodial part of the DATO and resentence the offender for the original offences to a non-custodial order.[^2777]

title: Non-compliance ‘sanctions’
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.2 – Sanctions, rewards, activation, and cancellation > 15A.2.2 – Non-compliance ‘sanctions’
text_marked:
If an offender fails to comply with a sanction involving a curfew order, community work order or order to remain at a specified place, the Drug Court must either:
• confirm or vary that order,[^2778] or
• cancel that order and take the first of the sanctions listed at (a)-(f) that it deems appropriate. This may include making the same kind of order.[^2779]
If the Drug Court is considering activating the custodial part under option (f), it must notify the offender, informant (or equivalent), and any prescribed persons about a hearing concerning the making of the custodial activation order.[^2780]
When making a custodial activation order, the Drug Court must specify the kind of secure custody facility in which the period is to be served.[^2781] The Drug Court may specify a youth justice centre as the secure custody facility if the offender is a young offender and it is appropriate to do so.[^2782]
Additionally, an offender can only be required to serve a period in a secure custody facility under option (f) if the period ordered or the total term of multiple unserved activated custody periods is at least seven days.[^2783] This means that while option (f) allows the Drug Court to activate between one and seven days of the custodial part of the order for each breach of a condition, in practice the offender will not serve less than seven days of the activated sentence at a time, once the activation orders for different breaches are accumulated.
A sanction for non-compliance can be made on the Drug Court’s own initiative or on an application by the informant, police prosecutor, prosecution, or certain prescribed persons.[^2784]

path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.2 – Sanctions, rewards, activation, and cancellation > 15A.2.3 – Compliance rewards
text_marked:
The Drug Court may on its own initiative confer one or more ‘rewards’ on an offender who is or has been fully or substantially compliant with the conditions attached to their DATO,[^2785] including:
• varying the treatment and supervision part of the order by adding or removing program conditions[^2786]
• varying one or more of the core conditions (other than the condition not to re-offend) or program conditions by reducing their frequency or degree[^2787]
• varying or cancelling a curfew order[^2788]
• varying or cancelling an order that the offender perform up to 20 hours of unpaid community work[^2789]
• varying or cancelling an order that the offender remain at a specified place other than a secure custody facility[^2790] or
• where an offender is yet to serve an activated period of between one and seven days under s 18ZL(1)(f) the Drug Court may de-activate some or all of the activated period,[^2791] or
• conferring any other reward it considers appropriate.[^2792]
‘Graduation’ Where an offender has fully or substantially complied with the conditions attached to their DATO and the continuation of the DATO is no longer necessary to meet the purposes for which it was imposed, the Drug Court may, on its own initiative as a reward, cancel the remainder of the DATO, including the custodial part.[^2793]
However, the Drug Court must not do so if the program conditions have already ceased operation.[^2794] Where the Drug Court cancels the DATO as a reward, any earlier orders activating the custodial part of the DATO cease to have effect.[^2795]

title: Maximum custodial activation period
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.2 – Sanctions, rewards, activation, and cancellation > 15A.2.4 – Activation and cancellation > 15A.2.4.1 – Maximum custodial activation period
text_marked:
When the Drug Court activates the custodial period of a DATO, it must first calculate the remaining custodial part.[^2798] The Drug Court can in its discretion order the offender to serve a period shorter than the remaining custodial part but it cannot order the offender to serve a period longer than the remaining custodial part. The maximum possible remaining custodial part for both the County and Magistrates’ Court[^2799] is:
• two years minus the period during which the treatment and supervision part of the order has already operated, if the original custodial part was no more than two years.[^2800]
• the original custodial part minus the period during which the treatment and supervision part of the order has already operated, if the original custodial part was more than two years.[^2801]
Up to that maximum, the remaining custodial part is the length of the original custodial part minus:
• each period of custody declared as having already been served under the DATO sentence, and
• each period of custody served in a secure custody facility under s 18ZL(1)(f).[^2802]
For example, if the original custodial part of a DATO is eight months and the court decides to activate the custodial part 18 months after it was made, it should first identify the maximum remaining custodial part. As eight months is less than two years the calculation to be made is two years less 18 months (being the duration for which the treatment and supervision part has already operated). Thus, the maximum remaining custodial part is six months.

text_marked:
Assuming the offender has served 14 days as declared pre-sentence detention and has served 16 days in a secure custody facility under s 18ZL(1)(f), the remaining custodial part is the length of the original custodial part, eight months, less one month (being 14 days PSD + 16 days secure custody). Thus, the remaining custodial part is seven months. However, as seven months is above the maximum possible remaining custodial part it must be reduced to the maximum of six months. The effect of the rules in s 18ZE(2)(a) is that the court cannot subsequently activate periods of custody already served as pre-sentence detention declared under s 18, or as sanction time under s 18ZL(1)(f).
The effect of the rules in s 18ZE(2A) and (2B) is that in some cases, but not all, the maximum period of custody that may be activated will be reduced by reference to the period during which the treatment and supervision part of the order has operated. This occurs where the operational days of the treatment and supervision part added to the days of the remaining custodial period exceed the relevant statutory limit (either two years, or the length of the custodial part). The maximum period of custody that may be imposed must then be reduced by the number of excess days. It is not reduced by the total number of operational days of the treatment and supervision part. These are complicated calculations, and in the County Court Drug Court Division, prosecutors commonly assist the judge with a formal calculation table. In other words, the court may choose to activate a period less than the remaining custodial part. title: Cancellation
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.2 – Sanctions, rewards, activation, and cancellation > 15A.2.4 – Activation and cancellation > 15A.2.4.2 – Cancellation
text_marked:
Sections 18ZN(1)(b) and 18ZP(2) deal with cancelling the treatment and supervision part of a DATO.
Cancelling the treatment and supervision part involves the exercise of a judicial discretion.[^2808]
Under s 18ZN(1), cancellation is available if the offender breaches a DATO by committing an offence punishable by at least 12 months imprisonment.
Under s 18ZP(1), the Drug Court can cancel a DATO if it is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that one of the following apply:
• the offender’s circumstances were not accurately presented prior to the order being made
• the offender will not be able to comply with a condition attached to the order because the circumstances of the offender have materially changed since it was made
• the offender is no longer willing to comply with one or more of the attached conditions
• the continuation of the treatment and supervision part is not likely to achieve one or more of the purposes for which the order was made, or
• the offender has breached a curfew order, community work order or order to remain at a specified place.
Section 18ZP creates a two-step process for cancelling a DATO. The first step is to decide whether one of the criteria (a)–(e) above have been proved and, if so, whether cancelling the DATO is warranted. The Drug Court has a residual discretion if the criteria are met, and may take into account the offender’s past compliance, the purpose of the DATO (including its rehabilitative focus) and any special circumstances present in the case.[^2809] For this purpose, compliance is not measured simply by how long the treatment and supervision part has operated – the Drug Court assesses the offender’s efforts to rehabilitate and participate in the program, and evidence of any lack of effort and commitment.[^2810] The focus is on events occurring while the DATO has been in force, and the cancellation process is not an opportunity to re-evaluate matters that were relevant to the original sentence.[^2811]

title: Cancellation
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.2 – Sanctions, rewards, activation, and cancellation > 15A.2.4 – Activation and cancellation > 15A.2.4.2 – Cancellation
text_marked:
When deciding whether to cancel a DATO for unwillingness to comply,[^2812] the Drug Court should consider the offender’s subjective willingness to comply with one or more of the conditions.[^2813] In DPP v Jurd, the Court of Appeal stated:
Although there is a conceptual difference between an offender’s subjective willingness to comply and a compromised ability to comply due to the dependency itself or for some other reason, past non-compliance and the risk of future non-compliance may provide a factual basis to infer a lack of willingness on the part of the offender to comply with one or more conditions attached to an order. In that way, there may be a relationship between a present willingness to comply and past non-compliance. But the two should not be conflated.[^2814]
This distinction between subjective willingness to comply and demonstrated capacity to comply reflects the legislative recognition that an offender’s dependency may affect their ability to comply with the order.[^2815]
The court also stated that it would be erroneous to treat s 18ZP(1)(c) as providing a power to sanction an offender in the event of serious non-compliance.[^2816]
But repeated non-compliance with conditions may show that the order is not likely to achieve its purpose/s and may therefore engage the power to cancel under s 18ZP(1)(d).[^2817]
The second step only arises once the Drug Court has decided to cancel the order. At this step, the Drug Court decides whether to: • activate some or all of the custodial part of the order, or
• re-sentence the offender for each offence for which the DATO was originally imposed, other than by imposing a term of imprisonment.[^2818]

text_marked:
In deciding which option to exercise, the Drug Court must first calculate the remaining custodial part[^2819] and must take into account the extent to which the offender complied with the DATO.[^2820] If the court decides to activate some or all of the custodial part of the order it may only activate a period less than or equal to the remaining custodial part calculated.[^2821] Separate procedural fairness obligations apply at each stage of the two-step process. The parties require an adequate opportunity to call evidence and make submissions on both the decision to cancel and the decision on what to do if the treatment and supervision order is cancelled. This does not necessarily require the Drug Court to make a decision on the first step and then hear submissions on the second step. There are overlapping considerations that apply at each step. However, it is preferable that the Drug Court adopt a two-step process.[^2822]
If the Drug Court re-sentences the offender, it cannot impose a sentence of imprisonment.[^2823]
The Drug Court must notify the offender, informant (or equivalent), and any prescribed persons about a hearing concerning the cancellation of the treatment and supervision part.[^2824] Further, the Drug Court must give reasons for a decision or order that adversely affects a person, including a conclusion that an offender is unable to complete the order thereby justifying its cancellation.[^2825]

title: Eligibility and limits
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.3 – Eligibility and limits
text_marked:
An offender is only eligible for a DATO if:
• they plead guilty to at least one offence punishable by imprisonment within the jurisdiction of the Drug Court[^2826]
• the offender is convicted of the offence[^2827]
• the court is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the offender is dependent on drugs or alcohol and that their dependency contributed to the commission of the offence[^2828]
• the court considers that if it were not to make a DATO it would be appropriate to impose a sentence of imprisonment (of no more than 4 years if in the County Court and no more than 2 years if in the Magistrates’ Court) that would not be wholly or partly suspended[^2829]
• the court has ordered and received a drug and alcohol treatment order assessment report relating to the offender[^2830]
• the court considers it appropriate in all the circumstances to make a DATO[^2831] and
• the offender agrees in writing to the court making the order and to comply with the treatment and supervision part of the order.[^2832]
A DATO cannot be made where:
• the offence:
• is a schedule 1 sexual offence[^2833]
• involves the infliction of actual bodily harm[^2834]
• is covered by ss 10, 10AA, 10AB, 10AC, 10AD or 10AE of the Act[^2835]
• the offender is subject to parole,[^2836] or
• the offender is subject to a sentence of a higher court.[^2837]
A DATO can be issued regardless of whether:
• an offender has previously been sentenced to imprisonment,[^2838] or
• an offender’s drug or alcohol dependency has previously contributed to other offending, or previous failures to comply with conditions of bail or sentence.[^2839]
A DATO can be applied across multiple offences.[^2840] However, an offender can only be subject to one DATO at any given time.[^2841]

title: Drug and alcohol treatment order assessment report
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.3 – Eligibility and limits > 15A.3.1 – Drug and alcohol treatment order assessment report
text_marked:
If the Drug Court is considering making a DATO it must first order a drug and alcohol treatment order assessment report to establish the offender’s suitability for a DATO and adjourn the proceedings until the report is prepared.[^2842] If the assessment report finds the offender is suitable for a DATO, the report will also provide a case management plan, identify the facilities required to implement the plan and make recommendations to the Drug Court on appropriate program conditions.[^2843]
The drug and alcohol assessment report may cover any of the following:
• the offender’s age[^2844]
• the offender’s social history and background[^2845]
• the offender’s medical and psychiatric history, including any treatment the offender has undergone for drug or alcohol dependency[^2846]
• the offender’s educational background[^2847]
• the offender’s employment history[^2848]
• the circumstances of any other offending for which the offender has been found guilty[^2849]
• the extent of the offender’s compliance with previous or current sentences[^2850]
• the offender’s financial circumstances[^2851]
• the offender’s housing history and needs[^2852]
• any special needs of the offender[^2853]
• any course, program, treatment, therapy or other assistance that could be available to the offender and from which they may benefit,[^2854] and
• any other matter the Drug Court directed that the report include.[^2855]
A Drug Court officer must file the report with the Drug Court and provide a copy to the prosecutor and the offender’s legal practitioner within a reasonable time.[^2856] They must also provide the offender with a copy of the report if the Drug Court directed them to do so.[^2857]
A party may contest a report by filing a notice of intention.[^2858] The Drug Court must then allow that party to lead evidence on the disputed matter and cross-examine the Drug Court officer about the contents of the report.[^2859] The Drug Court must not take the disputed report or disputed part of the report into consideration when making a DATO until this process is complete.[^2860]

title: Consent
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.3 – Eligibility and limits > 15A.3.2 – Consent
text_marked:
The Drug Court cannot make a DATO without the informed written consent of the offender.[^2861]
If the Drug Court decides not to impose a DATO, it must either:
• obtain the offender’s consent to continue with the sentencing matter and sentence them in relation to the offence/s,[^2862] or
• adjourn the matter for sentencing to the relevant non-Drug Court jurisdiction.[^2863]
Drug Courts have decided not to make a DATO where:
• the offender has repeatedly failed to attend for a DATO suitability assessment and subsequently threatened staff[^2864]
• the offender, due to the imminent birth of her child and the caring needs a newborn would require, was unable to meet the physical and appointment requirements of a DATO[^2865]
• the offender would spend a significant portion of their time living at an address outside the gazetted area[^2866]
• the assessor concluded it would be inappropriate due to the offender’s previous non-compliance with Drug Treatment Orders, coupled with the fact that the otherwise appropriate sentence was in excess of 4 years[^2867] • imposing a DATO would be too intensive given the comprehensive wraparound services already being provided to the offender (“overservicing”).[^2868]

title: DATOs and subsequent charges
path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.4 – DATOs and subsequent charges
text_marked:
Where an offender who is subject to a DATO is charged with a further offence (regardless of whether the offence occurred before or after the DATO was imposed) the Drug Court which made the DATO may hear the fresh offence.[^2869] The Act sets out a four-stage process.
• Firstly, the Drug Court determines whether it will deal with the new offence.
• Secondly, if the Drug Court determines it will, then it hears and determines the fresh matter.
• Thirdly, if the Drug Court sentences the offender to an immediate term of imprisonment for the new offence, the Drug Court must decide whether the sentence be subsumed[^2870] within the remaining length of the custodial part of the DATO (if that is possible, given the length of the new sentence and the remaining custodial part of the DATO)
• Finally, if the Drug Court decides not to order the sentence be subsumed, or the sentence cannot be subsumed, the Drug Court must cancel the treatment and supervision part of the DATO and either activate some or all of the remaining custodial part of the DATO under s 18ZN(1)(b)(i) or re-sentence the offender to a non-custodial order under s 18ZN(1)(b)(ii).[^2871]
This process will apply to a DATO participant in the Magistrates’ Court charged with an offence within the jurisdiction of the Magistrates’ Court (i.e., summary or triable summarily),[^2872] and to a County Court participant charged with an offence within the jurisdiction of the County Court (i.e., indictable only).[^2873]
However, if a County Court participant is charged with an offence within the jurisdiction of the Magistrates’ Court (summary or triable summarily), the Magistrates’ Court has no jurisdiction to hear the charge and must transfer it to the County Court Drug Court for sentencing.[^2874]

title: Mandatory disqualification
path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.1 – Mandatory disqualification
text_marked:
Mandatory licence disqualification follows if an offender has been found guilty or convicted of a serious motor vehicle offence,[^2877] which includes: • manslaughter arising out of the driving of a motor vehicle;[^2878]
• negligently causing serious injury arising out of the driving of a motor vehicle;[^2879]
• intentionally exposing an emergency worker, a custodial officer or a youth justice custodial worker to risk by driving;[^2880]
• intentionally exposing an emergency worker, a custodial officer or a youth justice custodial worker to risk by driving, in aggravated circumstances;[^2881]
• recklessly exposing an emergency worker, a custodial officer or a youth justice custodial worker to risk by driving;[^2882]
• recklessly exposing an emergency worker, a custodial officer or a youth justice custodial worker to risk by driving, in aggravated circumstances;[^2883]
• culpable driving causing death;[^2884]
• dangerous driving causing death or serious injury;[^2885] • murder or attempted murder arising out of the driving of a motor vehicle;[^2886] or
• any of the following offences, if arising out of the driving of a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or alcohol and a drug (‘substance-influenced offence’):
• intentionally or recklessly causing serious injury in circumstances of gross violence;[^2887]
• intentionally or recklessly causing injury or serious injury;[^2888]
• reckless conduct endangering life or persons;[^2889]
• statutory kidnapping;[^2890]
• common law kidnapping;[^2891]
• carjacking;[^2892] and
• aggravated carjacking.[^2893]
For dangerous driving causing death or serious injury, the minimum period of disqualification is 18 months.[^2894] For a substance-influenced offence (other than aggravated carjacking), the minimum period of disqualification is 12 months.[^2895] For any other serious motor vehicle offence, the minimum disqualification period is two years.[^2896]
There is no maximum period of disqualification.
Mandatory disqualification also follows if an offender has been convicted for:
• dangerous or negligent driving while being pursued by police;[^2897] or
• stealing or attempting to steal a motor vehicle.[^2898]

title: Mandatory disqualification
path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.1 – Mandatory disqualification
text_marked:
For dangerous or negligent driving while being pursued by police, the minimum period of disqualification is 12 months.[^2899] There is no minimum period for stealing or attempting to steal a motor vehicle, but there is a statutory default period of three months that applies if the court does not specify a period.[^2900]
A period of disqualification commences on the day the order is made, or on any later date specified by the court.[^2901]
The powers of the court in respect of the types of orders it may make depend on whether and what type of licence the offender holds at the time of sentence. Thus: • if the offender holds a driver licence or learner permit, the court must cancel that licence or permit and disqualify them from obtaining a further one for a specified period;[^2902]
• if the offender does not hold a Victorian driver licence or learner permit, but holds an equivalent licence or permit issued by another State, Territory or country, the court must disqualify them from driving a motor vehicle on a Victorian road for the equivalent period;[^2903]
• in any other case where the offender does not hold a driver licence or learner permit, the court must disqualify them from obtaining one for the equivalent period.[^2904]
A person disqualified from obtaining a licence or whose license is cancelled, suspended, or varied by order of the Magistrates' Court may appeal to the County Court,[^2905] and the Magistrates’ Court may stay operation of its order pending the decision on appeal.[^2906]

title: Discretionary licence disqualification
path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.2 – Discretionary licence disqualification
text_marked:
A court’s discretionary power to suspend or cancel driver licences or learner permits and to disqualify a driver can arise under two overlapping provisions. Firstly, the Act provides that a court may disqualify a person from driving or may cancel or suspend their licence where they have been found guilty or convicted of any offence, other than the mandatory disqualification offences discussed above or an offence under the Road Safety Act 1986 (Vic) (‘RSA’), or the RSA’s regulations or rules.[^2907]
The default period of suspension or disqualification is three months unless otherwise specified.[^2908] It commences when the order is imposed, or on any later date the court specifies.[^2909]
At the time of making the order, the court must enter in the records of the court that it is made under s 89A of the Act and state the offence(s) of which the person was found guilty or convicted.[^2910]
Secondly, the RSA provides that a court may disqualify a person from driving, or may cancel or suspend their license, where they have been found guilty or convicted of an offence under the RSA,[^2911] or any other offence ‘in connection with the driving of a motor vehicle’.[^2912] ‘In connection’ requires a substantial relation between the other offence and the driving of a motor vehicle, but not the manner of driving.[^2913]
If a person is disqualified under this provision, the court must specify the period of disqualification.[^2914] If a court disqualifies a person without expressly cancelling any driver licence or learner permit, they are taken to have been cancelled by that order unless the court specifies otherwise.[^2915]
While this order generally applies to all motor vehicle categories, a court may limit the order to specific categories if satisfied that the circumstances warrant it.[^2916]

title: Finding in respect of drug or alcohol contribution
path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.3 – Finding in respect of drug or alcohol contribution
text_marked:
When a court makes a licence disqualification order, it may make a finding that the offence was committed while the offender was under the influence of alcohol, a drug, or both, which contributed to the offence.[^2917]
This finding affects the person’s ability to re-acquire a licence and may make the grant of a new licence conditional on the installation of an alcohol interlock device.[^2918]
A court must make this finding where:
• the offender is found guilty or convicted of culpable driving; and • the culpable driving was constituted by the offender being under the influence of a substance to the extent that they were incapable of having proper control of a vehicle.[^2919]

title: Presumption of concurrency and interaction with the RSA
path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.4 – Presumption of concurrency and interaction with the RSA
text_marked:
Where an offender’s driver licence or learner permit is already suspended under specified provisions and their driver licence or learner permit is later suspended under the same provisions, the later suspension is presumed to be concurrent with the earlier suspension unless the court orders otherwise.[^2920]
This presumption does not apply if the RSA (or its regulations or rules) requires the suspension or disqualification to be consecutive.[^2921]
Separately, if the person has had their driver licence or learner permit suspended under Part 6B of the RSA, and the court orders that:
• their driver licence or learner permit is cancelled, and disqualifies them from obtaining one for a specified time; or
• the person’s driver licence or learner permit is suspended; the court must take into account that period of suspension in fixing the period of suspension or disqualification.[^2922]

title: Determining period of disqualification
path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.5 – Determining period of disqualification
text_marked:
Fixing a disqualification period is similar to exercising the general sentencing discretion. Aggravating or mitigating factors must be considered, as well as the competing sentencing principles and purposes.[^2923] A failure to give reasons for fixing the period of disqualification may indicate error.[^2924]
The period of disqualification commences on the date of sentence,[^2925] but its length may be fixed according to a defined event rather than being set as a fixed term of years. The usual event is the offender’s release from custody.[^2926]
Important sentencing considerations in fixing a disqualification period include:
• punishment and denunciation of the conduct;[^2927]
• protection of the community;[^2928] and
• rehabilitation of the offender.[^2929]
A court must consider the disqualification period’s effect on rehabilitation and whether the period fixed would be counter-productive to its achievement.[^2930] A disqualification period may be reduced to facilitate rehabilitation if necessary to transport for drug treatment,[^2931] meet CCO conditions,[^2932] or to obtain or maintain employment on release.[^2933] A court must examine the degree of dependency, particularly economic dependency, of the offender.[^2934] It may be inferred that the ability to obtain a licence once on parole will enhance an offender’s rehabilitation prospects, notwithstanding a lack of direct evidence.[^2935]
However, where no legitimate need for a driver licence is demonstrated, or where the offender’s prior criminal history involved unlicensed or disqualified driving, a longer period of disqualification may be justified.[^2936]
In imposing a disqualification period and its commencement date, a court should consider its interaction with other sanctions and the actual impact on the offender. A period of licence disqualification after release emphasises the punitive purpose of sentencing. Failure to consider the interaction with other sanctions and impact on the person may constitute error.[^2937]

text_marked: The impact of any disqualification period will vary substantially according to the sanction imposed. For example, a suspended sentence may mean that the disqualification will ‘bite’ immediately, while pre-sentence detention will mean that disqualification commencing on the date of sentence may extend further into the post-release period than intended. title: Confiscation
path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation
text_marked:
The Confiscation Act 1997 (Vic) (‘Confiscation Act’) is the primary mechanism for confiscating the proceeds and instruments of crime in Victoria, although there is other legislation that may also require a court to make a confiscation order.[^2940] A confiscation order may take a variety of forms. A confiscation order is not part of a sentence. It is imposed in addition to the sentence.[^2941]
This chapter is included in this manual only because there are difficult questions about the interaction of confiscation legislation with the sentencing principles and purposes.[^2942]
Forfeiture – whether by order or automatically under the Confiscation Act or via the operation of another piece of legislation – can be a mitigating factor where it places an offender in a worse position than before the offending and so is punitive and deterrent.[^2943]
Because a confiscation order may affect the exercise of the sentencing discretion, it is best if an application seeking one is heard contemporaneously with or as close as possible to passing sentence.[^2944]
On appeal, confiscation orders are treated as if they were part of the sentence.[^2945]
To the extent separation is possible, this chapter is restricted to issues relevant to a sentencing court and to confiscation orders that may be imposed at the time of sentencing.

title: Available orders
path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.1 – Available orders
text_marked:
At the time of sentencing for a Victorian offence, a court has two primary options. Firstly, if an offender is convicted of a Schedule 1 offence (which includes a Schedule 2 offence) a court may, on application, make a forfeiture order for ‘tainted property’[^2946] or it may defer sentencing until after determining the forfeiture application.[^2947] A forfeiture order directs that the ‘tainted property’, or any part of it specified by the court, be forfeited to the Minister.[^2948] The order must specify the interests in the property to which it applies.[^2949] A court may also restrain ‘tainted property’ at or closely before the time of charge.[^2950] This prevents the accused from disposing of tainted property in anticipation of being convicted of the relevant offending.
Secondly, a court may, on application, make a pecuniary penalty order (‘PPO’) requiring the offender to pay the State a penalty equal to the value of any ‘benefits’ they derived from committing the offence.[^2951] The court has the discretion to reduce this by any amount paid as restitution or compensation,[^2952] and may also defer sentencing until after determination of the pecuniary penalty application.[^2953]

title: ‘Tainted property’
path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.3 – ‘Tainted property’
text_marked:
The definition of ‘tainted property’ includes property:
• used or intended to be used in or in connection with the offence;
• derived or realised directly or indirectly from such property; or
• derived or realised directly or indirectly from the commission of the offence.[^2956]
In considering if property is tainted, the Court of Appeal has made the following observations about the statutory definition:
• The term ‘used’ should be given its ordinary meaning – that is, employed or made use of for a particular purpose or end.
• The definition is wide and inclusion of ‘in connection with’ extends the definition of tainted property to beyond that used in committing the offence.
• Whether there is a connection between use of the property and commission of the crime is a question of degree and fact. There does not need to be a substantial connection, nor does it need to be shown the offence could only have been committed with the property.
• The nature, extent, and significance of the use of the property in connection with the commission of the crime are relevant to the court in determining whether to exercise its discretion to order its forfeiture.[^2957]
The question of whether the property was ‘used’ will often be decisive,[^2958] but the mere fact that an act was done in or on particular property is normally not sufficient to bring it within the definition of ‘tainted property’.[^2959] It is only when the property or some feature of it is turned towards bringing about the offender’s purpose that it can be said to have been ‘used’.[^2960] The more passive the property’s use, the less likely it is the relevant connection will be found.[^2961]
